name: Fuhrer Thumb
beta: Grade II alpine climb (50° snow/ice couloir); 5-7 hours summit day from camp (~9,000 ft); requires prior glacier travel experience, cramponing on firm ice, two ice tools competency; hazards include ice fall from Kautz Ice Cliff, rockfall, avalanche danger (early start essential), crevasses on Wilson and Nisqually Glaciers; best season April-June; technical skills: rope team travel, secure belay placement, avalanche awareness
overview: A narrower, steeper variation of the Fuhrer Finger, climbing the couloir immediately to its west before rejoining the Finger route on the west side of the Nisqually Glacier at about 11,500'.

current.approach: From Paradise take the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista, descend the Nisqually Moraine west to the Nisqually Glacier, cross glacier westward, ascend Wilson Gully/Wilson Bench/Wilson Chute on west side of glacier to Lower Castle camp, then continue northwest to Fuhrer Thumb couloir
approach_variant_names: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson Glacier to the narrow couloir
current.descent: Most parties descend the adjacent Fuhrer Finger or the upper Kautz and standard Disappointment Cleaver route back to Camp Muir and Paradise.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit with pickets for the couloir.
current.pro_needs: Pickets and team arrest; no technical rock gear normally required.

name: Kautz Glacier
beta: No guide-maintained trail or fixed protection; requires proficiency in ice climbing, short-pitching, and crevasse rescue. The technical ice pitches occur near 12,000 ft, adding fatigue to the difficulty.
overview: The Kautz Glacier is Rainier's classic intermediate route — a step up from the standard glacier slogs, with two steps of alpine ice in the Kautz ice chute that range from a short pitch to a few hundred feet each, depending on the year. It climbs the south side from Paradise via the Nisqually Glacier and Wapowety Cleaver area to a high camp around Camp Hazard, then takes the ice chute and upper Kautz Glacier to the summit. It's the natural first 'real' alpine route for climbers who have done the DC and want ice.

current.approach: Two approaches are used, both arduous. The Paradise approach (5,420 ft) follows the Skyline Trail to the Nisqually Moraine Trail, then a climbers' path along the moraine to about 6,300 ft, where several boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier itself; most parties rope up here, since the crossing threads through heavily crevassed terrain exposed to icefall from above and is genuinely dangerous in reduced visibility. From the glacier's east moraine there are two ways up onto Wapowety Cleaver: a flat traverse to the base of 'The Fan,' a gully with avalanche, rockfall, and steep-slope hazard, climbed directly to a bench at 7,300 ft; or a climb up the Nisqually/Wilson Glacier margin at 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft 'Wilson Bench.' From the bench, snow slopes lead to the ridge crest and a string of established camps at increasing elevation — Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft), and the Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft, the most common base for a summit push, with running water from mid-June on). The alternative Van Trump Park approach starts at the Comet Falls Trailhead (3,650 ft): follow the maintained Comet Falls Trail 2.2 miles (2,000 ft gain) to a junction, continue toward Van Trump Park another 0.6 miles to where maintained trail ends, then follow unmaintained social trails up a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, followed up to the Upper Castle (9,500 ft) where the two approaches merge — descending this line requires a saved GPS track to relocate the correct moraine and treeline trail junction, even in good visibility, per NPS guidance. Above the Castle, the Turtle Snowfield (slopes up to 45°) is climbed on its west (climber's-left) side, close to the rock ridge, since its center and climber's-right (east) side are threatened by ice and rockfall from above. Established high camps continue at Camp Hazard (10,800 ft, on the climber's-left side at the top of the Turtle Snowfield), the Rock Step camps (11,250 ft), and exposed Wapowety Cleaver bivy sites (13,100 ft, used mainly by parties planning to descend via the Disappointment Cleaver rather than reverse the Kautz).
approach_variant_names: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
current.descent: Descending the Kautz is a real technical descent, not a walk-off, and involves multiple rappels through the ice chute — typically two to five depending on conditions, ice quality, and rope length. From the top of Wapowety Cleaver, parties reverse the glacier line down through crevassed terrain to the top of the ice chute, then find easier ground to climber's-left/east to belay into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice. The upper ice step (commonly a short pitch up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice) is rappelled: the NPS route brief states this takes anywhere from one to three rappels depending on rope length and how many ropes the team carries, using 'Zero-Thread' ice anchors — a variant of the V-thread/Abalakov anchor chosen because it's equally strong but leaves no gear behind; there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this route, and the Park Service explicitly discourages leaving V-thread anchors in place between ascent and descent since they can melt out. Below the upper step, lower-angle snow leads to the lower ice step, typically descended with one to two more rappels on the same anchor style — so two to five rappels total through the chute is realistic for most parties on a single 60m rope, fewer with two ropes or more if short-pitching. After the chute, a fast, alert traverse back toward the Rock Step is required, since this stretch sits directly under the active Kautz Ice Cliff. Climbing back up through the Rock Step itself (awkward 5th-class moves protected by fixed rope and old slings on rock anchors) returns parties to high camp; from there it's a walk/glissade down the Turtle Snowfield, back across the Nisqually or Wilson glacier crossing, and out to Paradise (or back down through Van Trump Park). A significant number of teams instead choose the 'up-and-over' option — descending the easier, non-technical Disappointment Cleaver/Muir Snowfield line from the summit to Camp Muir and Paradise — specifically to avoid re-descending the ice chute and Rock Step on tired legs, at the cost of having to haul full camping gear over the summit.
current.detailed_rack: Per rope team: 60 m rope, 4–6 ice screws (for the chute), 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit, a couple of slings/cordelettes for V-thread or picket anchors.
current.pro_needs: Mixed glacier + ice protection: screws for the ice steps, pickets for snow, plus standard crevasse-rescue gear. No rock pro needed.

name: Kautz Headwall
beta: Shares the Kautz Glacier's long approach to Wapowety Cleaver, then diverges onto a more direct, sustained line up the Kautz ice headwall instead of the standard ice-chute crux; airy traverse pitches above the headwall are typically protected with long pickets.
overview: A steeper ice-headwall variation rising directly above the Kautz Glacier on the south side, giving a more technical finish than the standard Kautz Glacier route. The approach crosses the Nisqually Glacier to the west edge of the Wilson Glacier, ascends the Wilson Glacier to about 9,500 ft, and continues to the Turtle Snowfield, where good bivy sites exist on rock islands between roughly 9,500-10,500 ft. From there the route climbs to the 'Rock Step' at ~11,000 ft, a short technical rock band typically downclimbed via fixed rope (or rappelled) to gain the Kautz Glacier, before reaching the main ice headwall, a roughly 300-foot wall commonly climbed in two pitches with a 60m rope at up to about 50°, with the crux technical pitches encountered near 12,000 ft.

current.approach: From Paradise (5,400 ft), the most common approach follows the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, then drops west onto the Nisqually Glacier; alternatively climbers use the Comet Falls/Van Trump Park approach from the Comet Falls Trailhead (~3,650 ft), directly from the Nisqually entrance area. Either way, the route crosses the lower Nisqually Glacier and gains the Wilson Glacier, ascending to the Turtle Snowfield, with established camps at the Castle (9,200-9,500 ft) and Camp Hazard (10,800 ft, at the top of the snowfield). This is a glaciated approach requiring roped travel and crevasse-rescue readiness once you leave the Nisqually; water is available from snowmelt streams lower on the Comet Falls/Van Trump side but not once you're on glacier ice. The headwall itself typically presents as two ice steps separated by a band of lower-angle snow: the lower step runs around 35-40°, the upper around 45-50°, with individual pitches reported anywhere from a short steep section up to 400-450 ft of alpine ice (up to AI3 on the upper step, harder if thin). Rockfall and icefall from the Wapowety Cleaver and Kautz Icefall above are the main approach-zone hazards — move through exposed sections early and efficiently.
approach_variant_names: Paradise and Glacier Vista, across the Nisqually to the Turtle and Camp Hazard
Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
current.descent: Descent is normally either back down the Kautz Glacier itself (the way you came) or a carryover down the Disappointment Cleaver route to Paradise. On the headwall's ice steps specifically, with 60m ropes two double-rope rappels plus some downclimbing are enough to get back down through the steepest sections to the base of the ice pitches — rappel anchors on the ice steps are typically ice (V-thread/zero-thread) anchors, the modern standard, not fixed bolts — old ascent-placed threads should not be reused. Expect 1-3 rappels through the upper step and 1-2 more through the lower step. This is a snow/ice route with no permanent hardware. In marginal conditions, some parties place running belays or fix a line through the ice steps instead of full rappels, both for the descent and to assist less-experienced members. Below the headwall, the Kautz/Wilson Glacier descent back to the Turtle or out via Comet Falls involves standard roped glacier travel, not further rappelling.
current.detailed_rack: Same core glacier/ice rack as the standard Kautz Glacier route: 2-4 ice screws per person and several pickets.
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for the steep headwall
current.rope_note: 60m rope enables two double-rope (30m) rappels off the ice headwall plus some downclimbing to regain the base of the ice pitches.

name: Sunset Ridge
beta: Primarily a snow/ice climb rather than a rock route, with roughly 6,400 ft of gain over about 5 miles from the base of the route; climbers traverse the Puyallup and South Mowich Glaciers to reach a bivy around 8,500 ft below the ridge.
overview: Sunset Ridge climbs the long spine separating the upper Mowich Face from the Sunset Amphitheater on Rainier's remote west/northwest side. After the long Westside Road/Wonderland Trail approach to St. Andrews Park, the route climbs a series of steep 50-55° gullies and open faces; at about 12,800 ft the ridge forces climbers out onto the upper Mowich Face, which is followed on steep snow or ice to 13,200 ft before the route regains the ridge crest to Liberty Cap and the true summit. It's a long, committing outing best suited to fast parties comfortable with routefinding on glaciated, seldom-traveled terrain.

current.approach: From the Westside Road gate at Dry Creek (~2,900 ft, about 3 miles up Westside Road, which leaves the main road a mile past the Nisqually entrance), walk or bike the closed road about 3.8 miles to Round Pass, then follow the South Puyallup River Trail to the Wonderland Trail and on to Saint Andrews Park. Leave the trail and climb north through alpine meadows to the Puyallup Cleaver (passing Tokaloo Spire), then leave the cleaver at about 8,500 ft to traverse the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers into the Sunset Amphitheater.
approach_variant_names: Westside Road, Round Pass, St Andrews Park and the Puyallup Cleaver
current.descent: The usual way down is over the top and down the Disappointment Cleaver, across to Camp Muir, then the Muir Snowfield to Paradise; this is a carryover, so leave a car at Paradise or arrange a shuttle back to the Westside Road. Early in the season, a party that camps on Puyallup Cleaver can instead descend the Tahoma Glacier, or its Sickle shortcut that skirts the crevasses of the main glacier, and return to the high camp. Stay roped on the glaciers, and expect crevasses and icefall on both options.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit with pickets for steep snow; several ice screws for the upper Mowich Face; full crevasse-rescue gear for the long glaciated approach.
rack: 3 x 120cm slings (anchor extension on the upper Mowich Face finish)
Two ice tools, ice screws, pickets
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets; full alpine ice kit for the headwall
bivy: Bergschrund camp in the Sunset Amphitheater
current.rope_note: 60m rope with long slings reported for the upper Mowich Face finish shared by this route; 4-6 ice screws recommended for that section.

name: Tahoma Glacier
beta: Grade II-III alpine glacier route. Approach via Westside Road to Tahoma Creek Trail (listed as closed by the park: washed out and exposed to debris flows), ascending Wonderland Trail to ~5,600 ft, then climbing southern side of glacier with multiple diagonal traverses.
overview: A classic, remote west-side glacier route. From the toe of the Tahoma Glacier the route ascends a series of diagonal zigzags — first up the glacier's south side to about 7,200 ft, then traversing to the opposite (north) side by ~9,000 ft, with further traverses between sides up to roughly 10,000 ft. Above that, climbers turn north to about 11,200 ft to enter the 'Sickle,' a steep chute at the extreme left (north) edge of the glacier used to bypass the icefall below; it's climbed on its north side, keeping left of icy ridges, to a plateau around 12,600 ft, from which the route joins the upper mountain.

current.approach: From the Westside Road gate at Dry Creek Trailhead: Tahoma Creek Trail to the Wonderland Trail (~5,600 ft), then onto the southern side of the Tahoma Glacier. The Tahoma Creek Trail is closed — washed out, unmaintained and exposed to debris flows from the glacier — so the usual alternative is to walk the road to Round Pass and take the South Puyallup Trail to the Wonderland Trail, then go either south to Emerald Ridge or north to St Andrews Park and up the Puyallup Cleaver, dropping onto the glacier on a ramp near 9,600 ft below St Andrews Rock.
approach_variant_names: Westside Road and Tahoma Creek to St Andrews Rock, then the Sickle
current.descent: Reverse the route, or descend toward the standard Disappointment Cleaver/Ingraham route and arrange a shuttle back to Westside Road; a documented recent trip logged about 8,770 ft of net descent loss over a 21.5-mile car-to-car itinerary starting from the Westside Road closure.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit with pickets and a couple of screws for steeper icefall sections; full crevasse-rescue gear for the complex glacier.
current.pro_needs: Full glacier kit; pickets and possibly a second tool for the steep sickle
bivy: Puyallup Cleaver camp below St. Andrews Rock
current.rope_note: Standard glacier rope; late-season parties specifically report needing to rappel into and ice-climb out of crevasses rather than just cross on snow bridges.

name: Willis Wall
beta: Mixed alpine terrain requiring pins, screws, nuts, and cams; multiple lines/linkups exist (e.g., the East Rib, and 'Traverse of the Angels' style link-ups), but the wall as a whole is rarely climbed given the objective danger.
overview: A notorious roughly 4,000-ft north face — the headwall of the Carbon Glacier's cirque — capped by a 200-300 ft band of hanging ice (seracs) that has historically deterred most attempts and is the wall's defining objective hazard. Named for geological engineer Bailey Willis, who helped build the first trail to the Carbon Glacier in 1881. The wall's West Rib was first climbed in June 1961 by Charles ('Charlie') Bell, though credit for the first ascent was disputed for years; Jim Wickwire (who climbed the East Rib in 1963 and made the first winter ascent in 1970) later corroborated Bell's claim by comparing notes and photographs directly with Bell.

current.approach: Traditionally approached via the Carbon River Road to Ipsut Creek and the Carbon Glacier — but SR-165's Fairfax Bridge (the only public access to Carbon River) was permanently closed by WSDOT in April 2025 with no detour, making this a ~19-mile one-way wilderness approach via the Wonderland Trail. Park fire closures have also shut the Wonderland Trail on that side between the Carbon River and Sunrise; check current trail status before planning that way in. Many recent parties instead approach via White River/Glacier Basin, crossing the Winthrop Glacier over Curtis Ridge to reach the base of the wall.
approach_variant_names: White River, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop-to-Carbon traverse under Curtis Ridge
current.descent: There is no descent route back down Willis Wall — after summiting, parties descend the standard Emmons-Winthrop Glacier route to Camp Schurman and out to the White River trailhead (the same drainage as the approach, reversing Curtis Ridge/St. Elmo Pass, or dropping directly to Camp Schurman and down the Inter Glacier to Glacier Basin and White River, glissading where snow allows). This is a walk-off/downclimb on established glacier route, not a rappel descent — no fixed rappels are used on the Emmons-Winthrop line.
current.detailed_rack: Light, fast technical kit: two tools, ice screws, pickets, a single rope for simul/belays, full crevasse-rescue gear; speed is the main 'protection'.
current.pro_needs: Full steep alpine ice kit; speed is the primary safety tool
current.rope_note: A minimalist rack uses one rope (consistent with a 60m alpine rope); the route requires rappels off ice cliffs (e.g. ~75ft) using doubled strands off a single rope, plus an extra sling used at one rappel anchor.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: From the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,100 ft), follow the Snow Lake Trail past Snow Lake to Gem Lake, then leave the maintained trail and traverse southwest up the ridge toward the peak. A cairn-marked traverse below cliffs near 5,400 ft leads into a small basin below the summit block, from which a class 2-3 gully of steep dirt and heather (often partly snow-filled) gains the final ~400+ ft to the 5,835 ft summit. Round trip is roughly 13 miles with about 2,700 ft of gain, commonly taking around 7 hours car-to-car; the crux is route-finding on the cairned traverse and footing in the gully when wet or snow-covered.
overview: Mount Roosevelt (5,835 ft) is a rocky, twin-summited peak in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, rising directly above the west shore of Snow Lake about six miles northwest of Snoqualmie Pass. It sits two miles north of its taller neighbor, Kaleetan Peak (6,259 ft), and is often paired with it for a longer traverse day. Despite its modest elevation and prominence (roughly 275 ft), Roosevelt has a reputation among Snoqualmie Pass regulars as one of the more serious scrambles in the corridor: its only non-technical line is an exposed, essentially unprotectable class 2-3 gully on the southeast side, and the peak's two summit humps — a lower north peak and the true, higher south peak — have caused parties to turn around short of the actual top.

current.approach: Trailhead: Alpental Ski Area day-use lot at the end of Alpental Road, reached via I-90 Exit 52 (Snoqualmie Pass) — go north on Alpental Rd about 1.3 miles to the upper lot (~3,100 ft), the same trailhead used for Snow Lake, Denny Creek and Source Lake. Follow Snow Lake Trail #1013 about 3 miles (steady climbing through forest and brush) to Snow Lake at about 4,000 ft. Continue on the High Lakes Trail #1012 along the east shore and around the lake's north end roughly 2 more miles to Gem Lake, then pick up the unmaintained boot path on Gem Lake's west side that gains the ridge toward Roosevelt. From the ridge crest, the boot path skirts left (east) of a band of buttresses to reach a high snow/talus basin below the two summit humps, then a steep, semi-exposed climbers' trail leads to the base of the final ~20 ft Class 2-3 step — loose and essentially unprotectable, the route's crux. Be sure to top out on the higher, more southerly summit; the lower north peak is a common false-summit stopping point.
approach_variant_names: Gem Lake's west shore to the southeast gully
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent gully: from the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 step back to the ramp, then drop into the boulder field below it. Follow the trail/gully down to the open talus slope on the southeast side and retrace the boot path back to Gem Lake and the Snow Lake Trail. Parties combining Roosevelt with Kaleetan sometimes continue traversing south toward Chair Peak Lake instead — only worthwhile as part of the longer traverse, since it does not shortcut the return to Alpental.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack.
current.pro_needs: None.

name: East Slopes (via Airplane Lake)
beta: The east side above Airplane Lake is Mount Saul's standard (and effectively only well-documented) route: a long approach with a short technical finish. From the White River Trailhead, follow Indian Creek Trail #1502 up the valley, then pick up an unofficial, unmarked path that climbs steeply to Airplane Lake, directly below the east side of the peak. From the lake, either kick up the east slope and east face (a snow climb early in the season) or gain the ridge north of the lake through a saddle and follow it to the summit, finishing with class 3 scrambling on rock that is solid in places and loose in others. It is typically done unroped, either as a very long day or as an overnight with a camp along Indian Creek.
overview: Mount Saul is the fourth-highest point on Wenatchee Ridge, a spur of the Cascade crest in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It has a bare granitic summit with jagged rocks, a sheer northwest face, and a south side that drops nearly 4,000 ft to Indian Creek Valley in about a mile — the mountain punches well above its modest elevation for alpine character. There is no maintained trail to the top; climbers approach via the Indian Creek Trail from the White River drainage, then leave the trail near Airplane Creek for an off-trail scramble past Airplane Lake to the upper east slopes and summit rocks.

current.approach: Drive to the White River Trailhead (also called the Indian Creek Trailhead) at the end of White River Road/FS-6400: from Leavenworth take US-2 west 15 miles to Coles Corner, turn onto SR-207 (Lake Wenatchee Highway) for 10.5 miles, then continue on White River Road/FS-6400 for a final 10 miles to the trailhead (2,300 ft). Follow the Indian Creek Trail north/west, crossing the White River at the trailhead and Indian Creek near its mouth, for roughly 4.5 miles. Near Airplane Creek, leave the maintained trail and bushwhack/scramble about 2,000 ft up to Airplane Lake (this leg runs 1.5-2 miles); from the lake, continue off-trail to the upper east slopes and summit via one of the three route options. Round trip is roughly 16 miles with about 5,300 ft of gain; a logged first-hand ascent recorded closer to 12 miles and 5,000 ft via a more direct Airplane Creek line, taking about 7.3 hours up and 4.4 hours down. From Airplane Lake, three lines reach the summit: the northeast ridge (working around a hidden, non-obvious cliff band north of the lake), a direct ascent of the clean upper east face slabs, or a looser steep-talus variation. Favoring the drainage about a quarter-mile downstream of Airplane Creek reportedly avoids the worst of the brush on the bushwhack in.
approach_variant_names: Indian Creek Trail and the Airplane Creek bushwhack to Airplane Lake
current.descent: Most parties descend the same way they went up. At least one party notes an alternate ridge-descent option off the summit as an alternative to retracing the ascent line; whichever way is chosen, time creek crossings on Indian Creek/the White River for morning (lower, easier water) rather than late afternoon, when snowmelt runoff makes fords more difficult.
current.pro_needs: None — the east side above Airplane Lake is a class 3 scramble typically climbed unroped; a rope and rack are not standard gear for this route.
bivy: The Indian Creek valley camps and the Airplane Lake junction site
The east slope above Airplane Lake — no established camp
current.rope_note: Class 3 scramble; no route-specific trip reports found describing roped sections. Typical for this grade in the Cascades to go unroped.

name: Noyes Basin Route
beta: Grade I, Class 3 via Noyes Basin — an off-trail scramble approach with no glacier travel, distinct from the Low Divide and Seattle Creek Basin lines on the same peak.
overview: One of three documented cross-country approaches to Mount Seattle, gaining the summit via Class 3 terrain through Noyes Basin.

current.descent: Descend via the same off-trail scramble route; no technical rappels are documented.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection documented — unroped Class 3 scrambling with no glacier travel.
bivy: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha

name: Seattle Creek Basin Route
beta: Grade I, Class 3 via Seattle Creek Basin — an off-trail scramble approach with no glacier travel, distinct from the Low Divide and Noyes Basin lines on the same peak.
overview: One of three documented cross-country approaches to Mount Seattle, gaining the summit via Class 3 terrain through Seattle Creek Basin.

current.descent: Descend via the same off-trail scramble route; no technical rappels are documented.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection documented — unroped Class 3 scrambling with no glacier travel.
bivy: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie

name: South Slopes (Standard)
beta: Most parties base-camp at Seattle Meadows (~4,550 ft), reached via a multi-day approach up the North Fork Quinault River to Low Divide and then west into Seattle Creek Basin. From camp, climb scree slopes on the mountain's western side, cross over a ridge, and continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, finishing with a class 2-3 scramble on the east ridge/side to the craggy summit. Two other approach variants exist (via Noyes Basin, and a more direct line up Seattle Creek Basin itself), converging on the same upper-mountain scramble.
overview: Mount Seattle (6,246 ft) rises deep in the Olympic interior, about 7.5 miles southeast of Mount Olympus, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Its northeast aspect drops over 3,800 ft to the Elwha valley in only about 1.5 miles, but the standard scramble routes stay on the gentler south/west scree and talus slopes. The peak was named April 29, 1890 by James Halbold Christie and topographer Charles Adams Barnes of the Seattle Press Expedition, in honor of the city that sponsored their winter crossing of the range; it was first climbed in 1907 by Asahel Curtis, Grant Humes, and Lorenz Nelson while reconnoitering for a climbing club's first attempt on Mount Olympus. Reaching the base of the peak requires a long, committing wilderness approach from either the Elwha or North Fork Quinault drainages — there is no easy day-trip line to this summit.

current.approach: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, 16 miles one-way by the river trail and much farther by the ridge, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it is closed to vehicles at Madison Falls by a washout, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach, up from the North Fork Quinault side, follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack up onto the Mt. Noyes-Mt. Seattle ridge — expect slow going in heavy brush low down.
approach_variant_names: Low Divide and Seattle Meadows
Up the Elwha to Low Divide
current.descent: Descend the ascent line in reverse: downclimb the east ridge scramble back to the scree/talus on the east side, cross back over the connecting ridge, and descend the west-side scree to Seattle Meadows camp. The scree and talus are loose and unconsolidated in places, so downclimb carefully rather than trying to glissade or boot-ski except where lingering early-season snow makes it safe; rockfall onto parties below is a real concern on the looser sections.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is documented for this route — it is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no glacier travel per the published route description.
bivy: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble on scree/talus; standard scramble kit, no rope typically carried.

name: Southeast Ridge
beta: The standard/easiest and most commonly climbed route on Sefrit. From Ruth Creek, climbers cross the creek and bushwhack up through slide alder to the base of the 'Wall Street' couloir, a roughly 1,500-vertical-foot snow gully about 50 feet wide at 30-35 degrees. The couloir tops out on the Northwest Glacier at about 5,000 ft, crossed (roped, with pickets/flukes for crevasse hazard) to a broad saddle at 6,500 ft just west of the summit. From the saddle, parties either climb a steep, narrow chute due south to a notch just west of the summit pinnacle, or traverse southeast across a shallow snow bowl beneath the summit — the traverse exposes climbers to cornices and is usually roped with snow protection. The route finishes on the southeast ridge: a straightforward Class 2 scramble broken by about 100 ft of exposed Class 3 traversing near the middle. routeFt here (3,691 ft) is a computed total combining the couloir, glacier crossing, and final ridge scramble, since no aggregate route length is known.
overview: The classic north-side line: a steep snow gully ('Wall Street') gains the Northwest Glacier, which is crossed to a 6,500-ft saddle west of the summit, followed by a Class 2-3 scramble up the exposed southeast ridge to the top.

current.approach: Drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) to Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to a pullout near milepost 3, just past a creek flowing over a concrete weir (about 2,950 ft), well short of the road's end at Hannegan Campground. From the pullout, cross Ruth Creek (a log crossing has been used) and bushwhack roughly 45 minutes through slide alder and devil's club to the base of the Wall Street couloir.
approach_variant_names: Ruth Creek crossing near milepost 3, then the Wall Street couloir to the Northwest Glacier
current.descent: Reverse the southeast-ridge scramble to the 6,500-ft saddle, re-cross the Northwest Glacier, and plunge-step down the roughly 1,500-ft Wall Street couloir back to the bushwhack and Ruth Creek crossing.
current.detailed_rack: A light glacier/snow rack: 1-2 pickets and a rope for the glacier crossing and the exposed traverse beneath the summit; a small rock rack is optional for the Class 3 ridge step.
current.pro_needs: Snow protection (pickets/flukes) for the Wall Street couloir and the glacier-bowl traverse beneath the summit; a rope is commonly used for both the glacier crossing and the exposed Class 3 ridge traverse.
bivy: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road

name: Southwest Ridge
beta: The Southwest Ridge approach offers an alternative to the more commonly documented Northwest Glacier-Southeast Ridge route. This line ascends the southwestern side of the peak through mixed climbing and scrambling terrain.
overview: A steep, seldom-climbed 7,191-foot summit rising abruptly above the North Fork Nooksack River, about three miles north of Mount Shuksan in the Mount Baker Wilderness (Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Whatcom County). Sefrit is notorious among North Cascades climbers less for technical difficulty than for its approach: a brushy, pathless bushwhack up steep timber and slide alder to reach a short but genuine Class 4 ridge/gully system leading to the summit. First climbed in 1930 by Jim Irving and Brick Spouse.

current.approach: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR 34), and follow FR 34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead (do not confuse with the separate Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR 32). Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there is no bridge, and early-summer high water can make it difficult or unsafe to cross. Follow the old roadbed/Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for roughly 50 minutes, then leave the trail and make an ascending traverse onto Sefrit's west/southwest ridge, passing through/around a cliff band, to reach the base of the summit gully system. Above the cliff band, the summit gully splits into several forks; the leftmost fork (or the one just west of a snow couloir to its right) is easiest, and rock is generally solid low but looser near the summit ridge. Note a separate, lower-angle north-side line — via Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier to the SE ridge — is Class 2 with one exposed ~100 ft Class 3 traverse, and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak; don't confuse the two lines when planning.
approach_variant_names: Nooksack Cirque Trailhead at the end of FR-34, then an ascending traverse through the cliff band
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: down-climb the Class 4 gully back into the basin, then reverse the ascending traverse to the old logging roadbed and out Trail #750 to the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead. Some parties rappel the short crux step using pre-existing sling anchors rather than down-climb it — inspect any fixed webbing carefully before trusting it, as its age/condition is unknown. Re-ford Ruth Creek at the trailhead; water is typically lowest in early morning, so plan to finish the descent before afternoon snowmelt raises the level.
current.detailed_rack: Light alpine rock rack — small to mid-size cams (roughly 0.3-2 in) and a handful of nuts for the crux Class 4 gully; a single 30-60m rope is sufficient given the short technical section. Bring extra slings/webbing since some anchor stations rely on aging fixed tat left by previous parties.
current.pro_needs: Minimal to none.
bivy: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road

name: Hanging Glacier
beta: Via North Face approach or from Fisher Chimneys route (drop down White Salmon Glacier approximately 1,000 feet). Cross the NW Rib route to gain Hanging Glacier. Features nice mix of glacier travel and ice climbing up to 65 degrees. Connected to Crystal Glacier at upper margins.
overview: One of Shuksan's original technical lines, historically known as the '1939 Route' - the Hanging Glacier carried the first technical ascent of the mountain in 1939. It climbs the Hanging Glacier on the peak's north side, between the Price Glacier and White Salmon Glacier cirques, and is currently retreating like most Cascade glaciers, which is changing its character over time.

current.approach: Note: the Hanging Glacier/North Face approach lies in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley west of Price Lake, rather than on the Nooksack/Ruth Creek side with which it is sometimes grouped. Drive the Mount Baker Highway to Glacier, WA and get a backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center (required), then continue up the Salmon Ridge/Mount Baker Highway corridor to the small pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site. Walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From there, with adequate snow cover, descend northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier — this is where roped glacier travel typically begins, with crevasse hazard increasing through the season. Ascend the glacier and moraine to a bivy around 6,000–6,500 ft, below the first rock/ice barrier. From the bivy, traverse climber's left, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake (visible below to the north-east) and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier, to reach the base of the shoulder dividing the White Salmon and Price Glacier cirques (roughly 7,500–8,000 ft), where the technical climbing begins. Key hazards: brush/alder low in the White Salmon valley when the snowline has receded; open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier; and, especially in early season, frequent avalanches shedding off the true North Face — parties are advised to stay right of it during the traverse rather than drifting left onto the face itself. An alternate approach used by some parties climbs the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Upper Curtis Glacier, then descends about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverses the NW Rib to reach the base of the Hanging Glacier — an option from the standard Lake Ann/Fisher Chimneys trailhead rather than the White Salmon side.
approach_variant_names: White Salmon Creek from the old lodge site, up the White Salmon Glacier to the dividing shoulder
Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide, then down the White Salmon Glacier to the base
current.descent: From the summit, most parties tie into the same descent used off Price Glacier and the standard Sulphide route: downclimb/rappel the summit pyramid's gully system (natural horn-and-sling anchors, occasionally pickets — typically 1–3 short rappels on a single 30–60 m rope, condition-dependent) down to Hell's Highway (a ~60 m steep snow/ice step) and onto the Sulphide/Upper Curtis Glacier. Because this route's trailhead (White Salmon Lodge) is on the same north side of the peak rather than at Baker Lake or Ruth Creek, many parties then reverse west from the Upper Curtis, dropping back over the shoulder and down through Winnie's Slide (occasionally a single ~30 m rappel if icy) toward the head of the White Salmon Glacier, then plunge-step the glacier back down past the bivy site and out the same valley to the White Salmon Lodge trailhead — avoiding the long Lake Ann/Baker Lake shuttle that Price Glacier and Fisher Chimneys parties face. Watch for opening crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier on the way down, weak snow bridges late in the season, and brush/alder in the lower valley once snow cover thins.
current.detailed_rack: 6-8 ice screws and picket(s).
rack: Light rack to 2in cams, small nut set for the 5.6 summit pyramid finish
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for steep ice and serac terrain
bivy: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
current.rope_note: ~3,000 ft of snow and glacial ice with steps up to about 65 deg to gain the upper Hanging Glacier, then 4th-5th class rock to the summit pyramid; used as an AMGA guide exam route for its sustained, moderate difficulty.

name: Northeast Ridge
beta: Moderate rock climbing between 4th class and 5.7 gains the exposed summit block; it requires additional ice climbing lower down to reach the base of the ridge and complex alpine rock-finding higher up. It is generally regarded as an alternate finish rather than a fully independent line from base to summit.
overview: The NE Ridge of the summit pyramid is a harder, seldom-done technical finish (up to 5.7) used as an alternative to the standard pyramid gully by parties topping out from the North Face, Hanging Glacier, or NW Rib lines on Shuksan's north side.

current.approach: Typically reached after climbing the North Face or Hanging Glacier route to the upper mountain, or via the NW Rib between the White Salmon and Hanging Glaciers.
approach_variant_names: Up the North Face to the summit pyramid
From the Sulphide Glacier, across the Crystal Glacier
current.descent: Standard descent is via the Fisher Chimneys line — down across the Upper Curtis Glacier, then Winnie's Slide and the chimneys themselves to the Lake Ann basin — or reverse the White Salmon Glacier.
bivy: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
current.rope_note: A light rock rack on a 60 m rope, carried on top of the axe, crampons and glacier gear you are already wearing. This is an alternate finish rather than a line of its own: parties arrive at the base of the ridge having climbed the North Face or the Hanging Glacier, or the NW Rib between the White Salmon and Hanging Glaciers, so the glacier kit comes with you onto the rock and there is ice to climb lower down just to get there. The climbing itself runs from 4th class to 5.7 on the exposed summit block, harder and more sustained than the standard pyramid gully it replaces.

name: Sulphide Glacier
beta: From the campsites (about 6,200 ft for the lower camp), head north up the west side of the Sulphide Glacier up rolling steps. At approximately 7,600 feet, terrain flattens and route continues northeast toward summit pyramid. The finish climbs the 3rd-4th class central gully up the south face of the summit pyramid.
overview: The Sulphide Glacier is the most straightforward glacier route on Mount Shuksan and the standard line for many parties, especially as a ski mountaineering objective in spring. It climbs the broad southern glacier to the base of the summit pyramid, finishing with the same rock scramble shared by other routes.

current.approach: From the end of FS Road 1152-014 (~2,500 ft), the route starts on the Shannon Ridge Trail #742, an old roadbed heading northeast. Follow it about 2 miles to where the road tread gives out around 3,800 ft, then continue on the true trail, angling left through brush onto the open ridge crest. Roughly 0.75 mile farther (~4,600 ft) the trail reaches timberline, where continuous snow often persists into midsummer (crampons/axe are worth carrying above this point in early season). From timberline, follow the broad, undulating ridge crest through meadows and broken timber for about 2 more miles to a pass where a major north-south ridge is met (~5,400 ft) — the Sulphide Glacier and the summit pyramid come into view here for the first time. From the pass, continue up open slopes and snow onto the glacier's toe; established bivy sites sit at roughly 6,200 ft (lower camp: several dry tent pads, composting toilet) and 6,500 ft (upper camp: dry pads, no reliable water). Total approach to high camp is roughly 4-5 miles one-way with about 3,500-4,000 ft of gain. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and ascend the broad, moderately crevassed Sulphide Glacier — crevasse hazard increases through the season as snow bridges thin, so carry and know how to use crevasse-rescue gear — angling climber's-left toward the base of the summit pyramid at roughly 8,400-8,500 ft. Water is unreliable above timberline late in the season; plan to melt snow at camp, and expect the first mile of brushy old road to be a bit overgrown and easy to lose in low light.
approach_variant_names: Shannon Ridge Trail #742 (standard)
current.descent: Descend the same line: reverse the Sulphide Glacier back to camp, then the Shannon Ridge Trail back to the trailhead. Off the summit, the standard descent down the central gully of the summit pyramid is a mix of downclimbing and rappelling. NPS climbing rangers have reported parties periodically replacing worn rap rings and anchors in the gully, so expect a mix of fixed rings/webbing at established stations supplemented by natural anchors (slung horns) rather than bolted hardware throughout. Plan on roughly two to four rappels depending on snow coverage and season — more rock is exposed and more rappels are typically needed later in the season, while early-season snow often lets parties downclimb and plunge-step more and rappel less. A 60m rope reaches between all standard stations; a 30m works but requires linking some sections with downclimbing between anchors. Note that stations are generally spaced for ropes with normal stretch — thin static or RAD-line-style ropes may leave gaps that require short, unprotected downclimbs between anchors. When the gully is dry and snow-free (typically later in summer), some parties instead descend the Southeast Ridge (about 5.3 with selective route-finding, or 5.6-5.7 held strictly to the crest) as a scramble alternative that avoids rappelling — but this is sustained 4th- to mid-5th-class terrain, not a simple walk-off, and isn't always in condition. Once back on the Sulphide Glacier, re-rope for glacier travel and retrace the ascent track to camp, watching for softened or newly opened crevasses in the afternoon.
current.detailed_rack: A light rock rack for the summit pyramid plus full glacier rescue gear.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rock pro; glacier protection as conditions dictate.

name: Standard Scramble (Putvin Trail / Lake of the Angels approach)
beta: From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road, the Putvin Trail climbs about 3,400 ft in roughly 3.5 miles to Lake of the Angels, including a very steep, sometimes near-vertical headwall requiring hand-and-foot scrambling on roots and rock. Beyond the lake, skirt the north/west shore and climb alpine slopes and a scree-and-snow gully (climber's-right gully) to a roughly 5,800 ft saddle at the peak's northeast/east side. From the saddle, cross scree, grass, and rock slopes southwest and scramble the southeast slope/south ridge on generally rotten, loose rock (Class 2, locally 3 to 3+) to the summit. The route has three summit horns; parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true (south) high point. Snow lingers on the gully and saddle well into summer and is reported as firm/frail, so an ice axe is commonly carried into July.
overview: A rugged, three-summited peak (south summit is highest) in the southeastern Olympics within the Mount Skokomish Wilderness, straddling the Olympic National Park boundary near Mount Stone. Built of rotten Eocene pillow basalt, it is reached by a tough, largely off-trail approach and a loose Class 2-3 scramble to the broad summit block. The standard Putvin approach was never inside the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire closure; the Mildred Lakes trail reopened in July 2026, while the Flapjack Lakes side beyond the Staircase developed area stays closed for repairs.

current.approach: The standard-route trailhead is the Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of Hwy 101 and about 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake trailhead, at roughly 1,600 ft elevation. Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels, not Mildred or Flapjack Lakes - those serve neighboring Mount Cruiser/Mount Lena out of the North Fork Skokomish/Staircase side. From the trailhead, Putvin Trail #813 is unmaintained for its last ~1.6 miles but well-traveled and easy to follow when snow-free; the tread is notably steep and narrow with unstable footing in spots as it climbs through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles in, the trail breaks into the open, grassy Whitehorse Creek basin and continues up to Lake of the Angels (about 3.5 miles and roughly 3,400 ft of gain from the trailhead, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace), a scenic alpine lake sitting in a cirque below Mount Stone and the Skokomish massif - this is the last reliable water source and the standard camp for an overnight trip. From the lake, climb westerly up pleasant alpine/heather slopes to a broad 5,800-ft saddle at the northeastern end of Mount Skokomish. From the saddle, a boot path/way-trail contours south and southwest across scree, grass, and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn, before turning to climb the final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge. Total round-trip stats commonly cited are roughly 9-12 miles and about 5,000-5,100 ft of gain, with climbing parties reporting 3.5-5 hours up. Hazards: the narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread; lingering steep snow and real avalanche exposure on the upper slopes well into summer (reports note hazard even in August/September); and notoriously rotten 'Olympic choss' rock and loose scree/talus on the upper mountain and summit block, which is the crux of the route more than any single technical move.
approach_variant_names: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the summit scree/rock to the saddle, then back along the boot path traverse across scree/grass/rock benches around the south and east flanks to the 5,800-ft saddle above Lake of the Angels, down to the lake, and out the Putvin Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - there is no rappelling anywhere on the standard scramble route. The main descent hazard is the same rotten rock and loose scree that makes the ascent tricky: downclimbing the exposed class 3 sections near the summit ridge crest is generally regarded as harder and more hazard-prone than climbing them, and parties should stay well left/south of the steeper cliffy drop-off noted on the north side of the upper mountain (contouring too far right/north near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous — cut west over the ridge instead). Watch for rockfall onto climbers below on the scree/talus sections, expect residual snow in the gullies and on the traverse into early summer (ice axe/crampons may be warranted), and budget real time for careful downclimbing rather than assuming a fast glissade-style descent - one party logged about 2.5 hours from summit back to the trailhead, but that was in good, snow-free conditions.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for the standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow in the gullies.
bivy: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
current.rope_note: Typical Class 2-3(3+) Olympic scramble: side-hilling, contouring, talus, rotten rock via Putvin Trail/Lake of the Angels. Steep snow lingers in the approach gully/headwall into early summer.

name: Silver Glacier
beta: Classed as advanced scrambling with glacier travel followed by a short Class 4 rock step. Parties rope up for the glaciated section (crevasses and a bergschrund are noted) and carry a small rock rack/runners for the final step, which is on loose, lichen-covered rock. It can be approached from a camp at Silver Lake (via Silver Creek) or from Ouzel Lake (via Depot Creek and over the Custer-Spickard saddle).
overview: The Silver Glacier route climbs Mount Spickard's glaciated north side: a wide gully gains the Custer-Spickard saddle, then glacier travel crosses the Silver Glacier to a notch just below the summit, finishing with a short Class 4 rock step.

current.approach: Two camp options are used. Via Silver Creek: arrange a Ross Lake Resort water taxi (reservation required) roughly 25 miles up Ross Lake to a drop-off at the Silver Creek mouth (1,600 ft); a trail climbs the north side of Silver Creek about 2.5 miles to an old cabin at 2,900 ft, after which the route continues cross-country (occasional blazes) across slide-alder and forest slopes to the Silver Lake basin camp (6,763 ft). Via Ouzel Lake: use the Depot Creek approach (see the Southwest Ridge route) to Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft), then climb toward and over the Custer-Spickard saddle. From Ouzel Lake, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully to the 7,380-ft Custer-Spickard saddle and step onto the Silver Glacier beyond it. From Silver Lake there is no saddle to cross: walk round the north side of the lake to its south-west end, then south across moraine and snow, skirting a small buttress, to the glacier toe at about 7,400 ft.
approach_variant_names: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
current.descent: From the summit, down-climb the short Class 4 step to the sub-summit notch (~8,500 ft), re-cross the Silver Glacier (roping up as on the ascent) back down through its flat section to about 7,400 ft, then either return to the Custer-Spickard saddle (7,380 ft) and descend the wide gully to camp at Ouzel Lake, or drop north from the glacier toe over moraine and round the lake to camp at Silver Lake. No fixed rappel anchors are documented; downclimbing/glacier travel is standard.
current.detailed_rack: Standard glacier travel kit (rope) for crossing the Silver Glacier, plus a small rock rack and runners/slings to protect the short Class 4 step below the summit.
current.pro_needs: A small rack and a few runners are enough to protect the short Class 4 summit step; the bulk of the route's difficulty is glacier travel rather than sustained rock climbing.

name: Southwest Route / Silver Lake
beta: From Ouzel Lake basecamp at 5,640 ft, ascend northeast up broad talus gully toward 7,360 ft pass between Ouzel and Silver Lakes. Veer right onto talus to reach Southwest Glacier; cross glacier carefully avoiding crevasses. Reach 8,000 ft col on south ridge, descend 40 feet, and traverse rightward across open slopes to obvious snow and rock gully. Final approach follows south ridge on right-side until final 100 feet, then cross left for summit. Snow slopes steepen to 35-40 degrees near top.
overview: Mount Spickard is a massive, heavily glaciated peak straddling the Skagit/Fraser drainage divide just 2 miles south of the Canadian border, part of the Chilliwack Group of the Skagit Range. It is the 5th-highest summit in North Cascades National Park and the 16th-highest in Washington, and its roughly 4,779 ft of prominence ranks 9th-greatest in the state. The mountain is built of Tertiary-age gneiss; the Silver Glacier drains north over a mile to Silver Lake, while a separate glacier system on the southwest side extends over 3 miles toward Mount Redoubt. First ascent is credited to Walter B. Reaburn in 1904; the peak's current name was applied in 1963 for climber Warren J. Spickard Jr., who died climbing a nearby peak in 1961. The standard Southwest Route/Silver Lake line climbs broad talus and a southwest glacier to a final short but loose Class 3 rock scramble, and is notable as much for its remote, cross-border approach as for its technical difficulty.

current.approach: From the Depot Creek Road washout (~2,600 ft, reached via a rough 4WD spur off Chilliwack Lake Road out of Chilliwack Lake Provincial Park, BC), the hike-in starts on the old roadbed: walk it about 9 minutes to an inconspicuous spur road on the left, follow that spur roughly 4 minutes to a T-junction, then bear right onto an extremely overgrown, sporadically muddy road for about 35 minutes to Monument 65 at the US-Canada border (roughly 45 minutes/0.8 hr total from the washout). From the border the route becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path following Depot Creek through beautiful old-growth forest - easy going where deadfall has been cut out, though dozens of uncut logs remain to step over in places. About 3 miles in, the path reaches Depot Creek Falls, the approach's real crux: crossing wet, slick boulders and slabs at the base of the falls. An old fixed hand-line was still serviceable as of a 2017 NPS trip report and assists at the vertical step here, but it should be treated with caution and backed up if in doubt - this is the approach's primary hazard, especially with a pack on wet rock. Above the falls the path continues through Depot Creek Meadow and Upper Depot Creek to Ouzel (Silver) Lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat, sandy, mostly treeless benches that serve as the standard base camp for both Spickard and neighboring Mount Redoubt, about 5-6 miles and roughly 6 hours of hiking from the road-end washout; Depot Creek and Ouzel Lake itself provide reliable water throughout. From camp, gain the climbing route by ascending a broad talus couloir and stream drainage north/northeast toward the ~7,200 ft Silver Lake saddle; well before the actual pass, cut right around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather-and-moraine basins and traverse to the toe of the Southwest Glacier, roughly 2.5 hours above camp. Rope up and don crampons/crevasse gear here: the glacier's climber's-right margin offers a line of hard 30-40 degree snow/ice with relatively few crevasses, but roughly halfway up, one distinctly 'inhospitable-looking' crevasse must be crossed on a marginal snowbridge - probe it carefully and be prepared for the bridge to have deteriorated depending on the season. A short, steep, loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on the ~8,000 ft col on Spickard's southwest ridge, the start of the summit scramble (easy 3rd-class rock and up to ~35-40 degree snow to the summit ridge). In early July a ditch cut across the road about a mile short of the trail start can stop low-clearance cars; budget extra walking if you cannot cross it.
approach_variant_names: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
current.descent: The standard descent simply reverses the ascent line - there is no separate descent route and no rappelling on the Southwest Route. From the summit, downclimb the short scree chute and traverse back across to the east side of the crest, then reverse the short section of Class 2-3 gullies, chimneys, and rock ribs down to the notch/col on the southwest ridge. From the col, downclimb the short, steep, loose rock step back onto the head of the Southwest Glacier and re-rope for glacier travel. Descend the same climber's-right line of 30-40 degree snow/ice, re-crossing (or finding an alternate line around) the marginal snowbridge over the mid-glacier crevasse encountered on the way up - glacier conditions and bridge integrity can change meaningfully between morning ascent and afternoon descent, so reassess rather than assuming the same line is safe. Off the glacier, reverse the traverse across heather and moraine slopes and descend the talus couloir/stream drainage back to Ouzel Lake camp; from there, retrace Depot Creek trail (re-crossing at Depot Creek Falls via the fixed hand-line) back to the Depot Creek Road washout. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent: no fixed rappel anchors exist anywhere on the route per every trip report reviewed - the rope carried is solely for glacier travel and crevasse rescue, not rappelling. The steep, loose rock in the summit gullies and at the glacier-head gully step is the main descent-specific hazard; a party could choose to belay or hand-line a member down the loosest short step near the col if conditions or skill warrant, but this is not standard practice and no such anchor is established.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit plus a few small pieces and slings for the short summit rock.
current.pro_needs: Roped glacier travel and steep snow, then exposed Class 3 scrambling to the summit; minimal rock pro.

name: Monitor Ridge
beta: Begin at Climbers' Bivouac (3,700 ft) on Ptarmigan Trail #216A. Hike 2.1 miles through forest and meadows to the Loowit Trail junction at approximately 4,800 feet, gaining 1,000 feet. Above timberline, follow wooden cairn markers up rocky Monitor Ridge through boulder fields covered in abrasive ash pumice. The final section features sandy terrain nicknamed the 'Vertical Beach' before reaching the crater rim at 8,363 feet.
overview: Monitor Ridge is the standard summer route up Mount St. Helens — a non-technical but strenuous scramble from the Climbers Bivouac to the crater rim, gaining about 4,600 feet over wooded trail, open boulder ridges, and ash slopes. The reward is a dramatic perch on the rim looking down into the still-steaming 1980 crater toward the lava dome, with Rainier, Adams, and Hood ringing the horizon. A permit is required year-round.

current.approach: From the Climbers Bivouac trailhead (3,700 ft, the highest vehicle access on this side of the mountain, reached via FR-90/FR-83/FR-81/FR-830 from Cougar), the route starts on the signed Ptarmigan Trail #216A through open forest. This trail climbs a moderate 1,100 ft over about 2.25 miles to timberline at roughly 4,800 ft — the last shade and the last practical spot to filter water (a couple of small seasonal creeklets cross the lower trail; nothing reliable higher up, so most parties carry all water from the car). At timberline the trail ends and the route transitions onto the open volcanic slopes of Monitor Ridge itself: a broad rib of old lava flows flanked by loose pumice and ash. From here to about 7,000 ft the route is marked by a line of large wooden posts spaced across the rock — in fog or whiteout, losing these posts is the single biggest route-finding hazard on the climb, since a minor drift off-line can put you on steep, loose, off-route terrain. Above 7,000 ft (roughly the last 1,300 ft to the crater rim) the posts end and the climb becomes an unmarked scramble/boot-pack up steep, loose pumice, ash, and scattered rock — two steps up, one slide back is typical, and it's more efficient on the rock ribs of the ridge than in the ash gullies beside them. A Washington-permit (year-round, required above 4,800 ft) is checked at or near the trailhead. There is no technical climbing on this route — it is a long, steep hike/scramble — but full winter conditions (ice axe, crampons, and avalanche awareness on the upper slopes) can apply well into late spring.
approach_variant_names: Climbers Bivouac and the Ptarmigan Trail to the marked ridge
current.descent: Descent is the same Monitor Ridge line back to timberline and then the Ptarmigan Trail back to Climbers Bivouac — there is no rappelling on this route (0 rappels; it is entirely a walk-off/scramble descent). The critical descent hazard is at the top: the crater rim is corniced with wind-built overhanging snow/ice that has repeatedly broken away, including a fatal collapse and multiple large rim failures in recent years, so the Forest Service and USGS explicitly warn to stay back at least 30 ft (9 m) from the visible rim edge and never approach or stand on a cornice for the crater view. From the true summit, descend back to the false summit and pick up the wood-post line down through the loose pumice/ash upper slopes; below about 7,000 ft the marked posts guide you back toward timberline, but climbers should double-check they're following the correct post line on the way down, since it's easy to wander onto a neighboring, unmarked drainage in poor visibility. Depending on season and snow coverage, glissading is possible on sections of the upper mountain and can significantly speed the descent, but chutes are frequently thin, rocky, and mixed with bare ash/pumice patches later in the season, so glissading should be assessed conservatively (an ice axe for self-arrest is standard kit). Below timberline, follow Ptarmigan Trail #216A back down through the forest to the Climbers Bivouac parking lot.
current.detailed_rack: Summer: no technical gear. No rope or rock pro on the standard route.
current.pro_needs: None — Monitor Ridge is a permitted scramble/snow climb, not a roped route.

name: Standard Scramble (Marmot Lake / Duckabush approach)
beta: From Marmot Lake Camp (~4,400 ft) leave the maintained trail and follow a small creek up into an amphitheater on the west side of the peak; easy Class 1 slopes lead from the amphitheater to the summit. The multi-day approach up the Duckabush valley (roughly 21-23 trail miles one-way to Marmot Lake) is the real crux of the trip, not the summit scramble itself. An alternate approach from the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish side reaches First Divide, drops into a basin with an unnamed lake, and climbs the saddle between Mount Duckabush and Mount Steel before turning north along the ridge to the summit block; the park lists that trail closed between the Staircase Rapids Loop and Home Sweet Home since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026, which leaves the Duckabush/Marmot Lake line as the open approach.
overview: Mount Steel is a deep-interior Olympic summit in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, near Marmot Lake and the head of the Duckabush. It sits about 1.4 miles northeast of its higher neighbor, Mount Duckabush, and was named in 1902 for William Gladstone Steel; the peak's first recorded ascent dates to July 19, 1897. Because the Marmot Lake approach alone is roughly 21 trail miles one-way, Steel is a genuine backcountry objective that rewards solitude over technical difficulty.

current.approach: Start at the Duckabush Trailhead (FR 2510-060) off US 101 and follow the Duckabush River Trail #803. The first real test is Big Hump at mile 3.9: a steep, loose-rock push of about 1,000 ft in roughly 30 switchbacks, then a 800 ft drop back down to river level on the far side — this is the trail's technical crux underfoot, not the summit. Continue upriver through old growth and a burned section (standing dead snags — use caution in wind) to Five Mile Camp (5.3 mi), a popular water stop and camp at a set of rapids. Between the Olympic National Park boundary (~6.2 mi from the trailhead) and Ten Mile Camp expect scattered blowdown and a documented trail washout that must be scrambled around rather than crossed directly. Above Duckabush Camp (about mile 17.7), the trail fords the Duckabush River itself — a wide crossing that can run thigh-deep and swift in early season or after rain; scout upstream/downstream for the best braid and use a pole. From Duckabush Camp, continue upvalley roughly 3 more miles on the Duckabush/O'Neil Pass trail; the unmarked Marmot Lake climbers' route then leaves the maintained trail (no sign, occasional cairns at best) and follows a small feeder creek up climber's-left into a rocky amphitheater on the west side of Mount Steel's summit. This final stretch is cross-country travel over heather benches and talus, finishing on easy Class 2 slopes to the summit ridge and the 6,225-ft high point. Snow lingers in the amphitheater and on the upper slopes into summer, with nasty cornices reported on the summit ridge until late June, so carry an ice axe and expect firm early-morning snow before roughly early July. Water is reliable along the Duckabush and at Marmot Lake but scarce once you leave the creek for the amphitheater, so top off there. With Marmot Lake itself over 21 miles from the trailhead, this route is done as a multi-day backpack with a high camp at Marmot Lake or the amphitheater, not a car-to-car day climb. A second, reportedly easier approach starts from First Divide (13-14 miles from the Staircase trailhead via the North Fork Skokomish Trail): follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake, drop southwest to the saddle between Mount Steel's two summit humps, then finish north along the summit ridge; this line shares the same early-summer cornice/avalanche caution near the ridge crest. That approach is closed: the park lists the North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide, and First Divide camp, as closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on its trail-conditions page (updated September 14, 2026) or fire-conditions page (updated September 18, 2026).
approach_variant_names: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
First Divide and the unnamed lake basin
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: downclimb the Class 2 talus/heather slopes and any lingering snow back through the amphitheater to the feeder creek, rejoin the Duckabush/O'Neil Pass trail, and retrace Trail #803 the full distance to the trailhead. This is a non-technical scramble route with no established rappel stations and no rock protection reported on any route description found — no rappelling is required; treat any steep snow patches with an ice axe/self-arrest rather than a rope. The two real hazards on the way out are the Duckabush ford just above Duckabush Camp (worse in the afternoon with elevated snowmelt flow than on an early-morning crossing) and the loose, steep switchbacks of Big Hump on tired legs — most parties split the roughly 21+ mile walk-out with a second night at Five Mile Camp or Ten Mile Camp rather than pushing straight through.
current.pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line.
bivy: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
current.rope_note: Long approach (21 mi via Duckabush to Marmot Lake) then easy slopes to the summit block; wet conditions common June-early July.

name: Cascadian Couloir
beta: Class 3 rock when melted out in summer; a popular snow climb/ski descent in winter and spring. Bypasses several small cliff bands low in the gully.
overview: The standard, non-technical route up Mount Stuart and the standard descent for every technical ridge/face route on the mountain. From the false summit (~9,200 ft) it's a short, exposed Class 2-3 scramble east along the ridge to the true summit. Stuart is the unrivalled crown peak of Washington's central Cascades, and this route is the one most often photographed from Longs Pass.

current.approach: Drive to the Esmeralda (DeRoux Campground/Teanaway) trailhead at the end of North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), elevation ~4,243 ft — from I-90 exit 85 near Cle Elum, take SR 970 northeast, then Teanaway River Road roughly 23 miles to the road-end parking. From the trailhead, hike an old mining road/climbers' trail about 0.25 mile to a fork and take the right (east) branch toward Longs Pass. The trail climbs a mostly open, sun-exposed hillside — worth starting before dawn in summer to avoid the heat — gaining roughly 2,000 ft over about 2 miles to Longs Pass (~6,250 ft), the high point of the approach and the first place Mount Stuart and the Cascadian Couloir come into view. From the pass, descend the steep, loose scree on the far side, dropping about 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek. Cross the creek on a log footbridge, then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail east for about a mile to a meadow and campsite area around 4,800 ft (good camps are found straight south of the couloir's outlet, and a few more near the footlog); this is the standard basecamp for an overnight ascent, though the route is also done car-to-car. From camp, pick up the climbers' trail up through the meadow to the toe of the couloir and begin ascending. Water is reliable at Ingalls Creek and in the meadow below the couloir but is not available higher up, so fill bottles before starting the climb. Trailhead-to-camp runs roughly 3-4 hours; camp-to-summit another 5-8 hours. The Ingalls Creek crossing can run high and fast in early-season snowmelt, and the Longs Pass hillside carries some avalanche exposure in winter/spring conditions.
approach_variant_names: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble
Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb
current.descent: Standard descent is simply reversing the ascent line — a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling (0 rappels). From the false summit (~9,200 ft), descend the broken class 2-3 ridge back to the couloir, then work down the Cascadian Couloir itself, staying on the established climber's-left talus path around the permanent snowfield near 8,800 ft (parties who wander onto the right side of the snowfield have encountered old rappel-station remnants and much harder, more hazardous downclimbing — avoid this line). The couloir is notoriously loose top to bottom — sand, scree, and unstable blocks create real rockfall risk for parties below, and the upper sections splinter into a maze of use-trails and cairns that make route-finding genuinely tricky, especially at dawn/dusk or in whiteout; a GPS track or careful attention to your ascent line is worthwhile. An ice axe (and crampons in early season, or on any lingering snow tongue) should be carried for the descent through at least mid-summer. Continue down to Ingalls Creek, re-cross the footlog, and regain about 1,400-1,500 ft back up to Longs Pass over roughly 2-3 miles before descending the final stretch to the Esmeralda trailhead. Budget roughly 5-8 hours summit-to-car for this descent; it is also the standard descent for other Mount Stuart routes (e.g., the North Ridge) whose parties finish on the opposite side of the mountain from where they started.
current.detailed_rack: Non-technical in summer. No rope required for the standard line, though some parties bring a short rope for the summit block.
current.pro_needs: None on the standard scramble; a short rope is optional for nervous parties on the summit block.
bivy: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass

name: Girth Pillar
beta: The named pillar sits high on the northeast face above the Ice Cliff Glacier icefall. After the glacier approach and four easy pitches, three engaging crack pitches form the crux; large loose blocks are noted near the top of the pillar.
overview: A steep, clean rock pillar rising out of the Ice Cliff Glacier on Mount Stuart's northeast face, first climbed by Kit Lewis and Jim Nelson in 1983. After climbing the access ramp onto the upper Ice Cliff Glacier from the lower North Ridge, four easy pitches lead to the base of the pillar, followed by three sustained crack-climbing crux pitches, then easier climbing to the main false summit above the glacier — 11 pitches in all.

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Trail #1599, ~3,400') off Icicle Creek Rd/FS-7601, follow the trail up Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake junction (~4,600') and stay right for Stuart Lake. About a mile farther, leave the trail where it turns uphill for Stuart Lake: cross Mountaineer Creek on logs, follow the climbers' path up the valley bottom, and climb steepening talus and heather benches directly toward the basin beneath the Ice Cliff Glacier on Stuart's northeast face (moraine camps around 6,800-7,000'). This off-trail stretch is loose and exposed to rockfall — expect real route-finding, especially in the dark on an alpine start. From camp, rope up and climb the Ice Cliff Glacier itself: this is the route's main objective hazard, with significant icefall, spindrift, and crevasse danger — parties typically stay left to dodge falling ice and swing wide right to avoid the glacier's largest crevasses. At the top of the glacier is the 'ice cliff' step itself, anywhere from 10 to 100+ feet of 50-70° snow/ice (easier and shorter early season, steeper and more likely bare ice as the season progresses). Above the step, four moderate pitches of rock lead to the base of the Girth Pillar proper (~8,200-8,400'). There is no water source above the moraine camp — carry what you need for the climb, or plan to melt snow/ice.
approach_variant_names: Ice Cliff Glacier to the top of the ice, then four easy pitches to the pillar
current.descent: The route tops out on easier ground above the pillar, leading to the false summit above the Ice Cliff Glacier and on to Stuart's true summit. There is no reasonable way to reverse the route — down-climbing or rappelling back through the Ice Cliff Glacier's icefall and crevasse hazard is considerably more dangerous than finishing over the top, so continuing to the summit is effectively mandatory. From the true summit, retrace toward the false summit and descend the Sherpa Glacier, entered just east of where the Ice Cliff Glacier couloir tops out near 8,200 ft, back to the moraine camp; later in the season, once the Sherpa has melted out, parties go around Sherpa Peak to Sherpa Pass instead. Then walk out the Mountaineer Creek climbers' trail to the Stuart Lake trailhead, the same one used for the approach, so no car shuttle is needed. The glacier descent is technical, especially in the dark, so keep the axe, crampons and crevasse kit for it. If a party needs to bail from partway up the pillar itself, the crack pitches would need to be rappelled on natural gear anchors (no fixed hardware is reported on the pillar) — a real possibility to plan for given the route's commitment, but not part of the standard descent.
current.detailed_rack: Single to double rack of cams through hand size, a set of nuts.
current.pro_needs: Standard alpine rack emphasizing finger-to-hand cracks; light glacier kit for the approach.
bivy: Mountaineer Creek basin below the Sherpa Glacier

name: Kamikaze Trail (SW Ridge Scramble)
beta: Popular with scramblers and trail runners seeking a harder version of the peak. Features Class 2-3 rock steps, steep root/dirt tread, and minor exposure, with lingering snow near the ridge crest into early summer. Many parties ascend via Kamikaze and descend the standard trail through Rachor Pass to make a ~10-mile loop rather than retracing the steep boot track.
overview: A steeper, more direct line that leaves the standard trail near Teneriffe Falls and climbs a boot track up the mountain's southwest (Kamikaze) ridge, gaining roughly 2,300 ft in about a mile before rejoining the upper mountain near the summit — considerably more strenuous than the standard trail.

current.approach: Follow the Mount Teneriffe Trail from the paved trailhead on SE Mount Si Road to the signed Teneriffe Falls junction at about 0.9 mile, turn right, and follow the Teneriffe Falls Trail to the falls viewpoint at about 2.8 miles. From just below the viewpoint, the unofficial but well-traveled Kamikaze Trail boot track climbs directly up the forested southwest ridge/flank of the mountain, gaining about 2,300 ft in roughly one mile of steep, rocky, single-track tread before reaching the Kamikaze Ridge crest (~3,900 ft) and continuing to a cedar-grove shelf (~4,200 ft) that meets the upper mountain near the summit. The trailhead gate was reported locked at about 8 pm and unlocked around 7 am in May and August, so plan a loop that finishes before then.
approach_variant_names: Standard trail to the falls junction, then the unofficial boot track
