current.descent: Most parties either carefully retrace the steep Kamikaze boot track (slower and more slip-prone heading down, especially when wet) or continue over the summit onto the standard Mount Teneriffe Trail, dropping to Rachor Pass (~4,200 ft saddle) and following the switchbacks back past the Teneriffe Falls junction to the trailhead for a loop of roughly 10 miles.
current.detailed_rack: No technical protection rack is used — this is an unroped scramble route.
current.pro_needs: None; sure footing and caution on wet rock substitute for any climbing protection.
bivy: Mount Teneriffe and the Mount Si conservation area, no overnight

name: West Ridge
beta: The West Ridge is Mount Thomson's most technical and aesthetic alpine climbing objective. The route ascends 4-5 pitches of low to mid-fifth-class rock on the west ridge crest, with the crux being a well-featured chimney on pitch 1 and a 5.6 bulge pull on pitch 2. Route-finding is generally straightforward once established on the ridge proper. Multiple belay options exist on comfortable ledges with solid natural anchors. The descent via the East Ridge (Class 3-4) balances the upclimb and includes one optional 20-foot Class 4 rappel.
overview: Mount Thomson (6,554 ft; spelled 'Thompson' in most published descriptions, 'Thomson' on USGS/Green Trails maps) is a sharp, Matterhorn-like andesite peak on the PCT divide roughly 4 miles northeast of Snoqualmie Pass, in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness (Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Snoqualmie Ranger District). The West Ridge is its classic technical line: sound, porphyritic-andesite rock, rated Grade II, 5.6, with a long wilderness approach that keeps it quieter than roadside Cascades crags.

current.approach: Park at the PCT North (Commonwealth Basin) Trailhead lot just off the frontage road at Exit 52, Snoqualmie Pass (~3,000 ft) — cross under I-90, take the first right, and the lot is on the right. From the trailhead, follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; it climbs steadily through timber via long switchbacks for roughly 5.5–6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk (~5,400 ft), a narrow, exposed ledge blasted directly into a granite cliff on the ridge north of Kendall Peak — solid underfoot but very exposed, use caution if icy or in high wind. Continue north on the PCT about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake (~5,260 ft), the last reliable water source and a common camp/rest stop (roughly 2–2.5 hrs / ~7 mi in from the car). About 0.4–0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching left (west) off the PCT; it climbs a steep ~200 ft to Bumblebee Pass (~5,400 ft), a small saddle above Alaska Lake. The path is loose and eroded in spots on both the up and down sides — take care with footing. Drop off the far side of the pass into Bumblebee Basin (scattered camps, seasonal water), then contour/ascend northwest across talus and scree (worse-looking than it climbs) toward the lowest notch on Thomson's west ridgeline (~5,960 ft). Short sections of 4th-class scrambling around a set of gendarmes lead to the notch at the base of the route, where the first pitch starts just left (north) of the crest. Total trailhead-to-base distance is about 8–8.5 miles with roughly 2,900–3,000 ft of gain, typically 4–5 hours for a fit party; most groups do the climb car-to-car in one long day, though the basin makes a fine camp for a two-day trip.
approach_variant_names: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the basin, then the lowest notch on the west ridge
current.descent: From the true summit, the standard descent follows the East Ridge back toward Bumblebee Pass rather than reversing the West Ridge climb. Walk/scramble off the east end of the summit block on a faint climbers' path to a notch where several parties over the years have left fixed tree anchors (webbing and rap rings, not bolts) at three points along the ridge's steeper steps — roughly around 6,200 ft and lower. Descent style varies by party and conditions: some downclimb the entire East Ridge unroped (sustained, exposed class 3–4 with a couple of low-5th moves), while most rope up for at least one section. A common approach is a single double-rope rappel (60m rope, doubled) off the initial tree anchor to bypass the steepest, most exposed step, then class 3 scrambling the rest of the way down; other parties describe using two to three shorter rappels off successive tree stations (doubled 8mm/thin rope, ~30m per rap) where the rock is loose or holds are wet, downclimbing the easier sections between them. Inspect any tat/rap rings before weighting them and back them up or replace old webbing if in doubt — these are climber-maintained natural anchors, not resupplied by any agency. Once off the ridge's technical ground, descend talus back into Bumblebee Basin, regain the steep boot path up and over Bumblebee Pass, drop back to the PCT near Ridge Lake, and retrace the Kendall Katwalk and switchbacks south to the PCT North Trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Cams roughly 0.5"-2" (a handful of small-to-mid sizes covers most placements), a set of nuts/stoppers, and about 6 alpine quickdraws/slings (most pitches take only 3-4 placements).
current.pro_needs: Light natural protection and minimal aid gear needed. The route is well-anchored on natural features. No bolts or fixed anchors on the route; all belay stations are at natural ledges with bomber rock for anchor placement (trees, blocks, cracks).
bivy: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk

name: South Ridge
beta: The South Ridge begins with an approach via the Taboo Glacier from Boston Basin high camp. After a short glacier crossing, climbers traverse under a spur ridge and ascend slabby terrain to reach the south ridge notch. The route follows the left side of the ridge via short dihedrals, ledges, and chimneys for roughly 1,000 feet to the summit. The final sections circumnavigate the peak via the southeast face with brief class 4 scrambling before reaching the airy northeast ridge summit.
overview: The standard route to Torment's summit, climbing solid granite over moderate steps and towers on four pitches (~1000 ft); best known as the start of the Torment-Forbidden Traverse. Climbing tops out around 5.4 with generally good rock and moderate route-finding.

current.approach: Start at the Boston Basin Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road/FR-15). The unmaintained but well-beaten climbers' trail switchbacks steeply up through forest and traverses west, crossing a couple of small creeks (reliable water), to reach the meadows of Boston Basin in roughly 1.5-3.5 hours depending on pace and pack weight. Established low camps sit around 5,300 ft on the basin's tundra benches; from there, continue climbing skier's-right of Boston Creek (a good water source until it's dry/frozen) up open slabs and tundra to the upper high camp near 6,400-6,600 ft, below Sharkfin Tower and Forbidden Peak's south spur. From high camp, do a rising traverse northwest at roughly the 6,200 ft contour, staying beneath Forbidden's south spur, cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, and continue toward the toe of the Taboo Glacier. Gain the glacier on its left (climber's left) side and follow it up until a deep gully/couloir breaks through the rock band on the left; a bergschrund or moat typically has to be negotiated here and has been the site of a fatal accident, so treat the crossing seriously, especially early season when it's snow-bridged or late season when it's wide open. Scramble up the gully (class 3-4, loose in spots — helmet recommended) to the South Ridge notch/South Col. Expect firm snow or glacier ice on the approach slopes early in the season (crampons/axe useful) and a short glacier crossing that warrants basic crevasse-rescue readiness even though it is generally low-angle and short.
approach_variant_names: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
Torment Basin climbers' path
current.descent: Three options exist, and the choice depends on party speed and whether you're continuing to Forbidden Peak. (1) Reverse the South Ridge: downclimb interspersed with numerous short, traversing rappels off fixed slings/anchors that are 'in abundance' along the ridge — a single rope is generally sufficient for these short raps, but carry extra webbing/cord to back up or replace tat, since stations are alpine-style (slung horns, chockstones, occasional old fixed gear) rather than bolted. This option is slower but avoids the moat problems of the SE Face line. (2) Descend the Southeast Face: downclimb from the summit area to the top rappel station, then make 5-6 double-rope (60m) rappels down the SE Face gully/slab system back toward the Taboo Glacier — the second station is on climber's left, the rest are straight down or climber's right. The crux of this option is the final rappel, where you must cross a moat/bergschrund to reach the snowfield below; this can be genuinely difficult and its condition can't be scoped from above, so the first person down should carry a picket, ice axe, and crampons to help climb out of the moat if needed. Bring two ropes (or a single rope doubled) for these double-rope rappels. (3) Continue over the summit and descend via the Torment-Forbidden Traverse toward Forbidden Peak (sustained exposure, a 5.6 step and ~45-degree snow/ice) if that's the day's objective — this is a full traverse, not a simple descent, and commits you to exiting via Forbidden's West Ridge/Boston Basin instead of returning the way you came.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from 0.4 to 2 inches, a set of nuts, about 8 alpine draws with slings for towers, and a 60m rope.
current.pro_needs: The granite protects well on the steeper steps with cracks and horns, with run-out moderate sections between. Slinging towers speeds protection on the exposed crest.
bivy: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins

name: Torment-Forbidden Traverse
beta: The Torment-Forbidden Traverse is a multi-day alpine adventure combining Mount Torment's South Ridge approach with a mile-long exposed ridge traverse to neighboring Forbidden Peak (8,815 ft), finishing via the famous Forbidden West Ridge (5.7, 50 classic). The route crosses the Taboo Glacier, climbs to Mount Torment's summit via the south ridge, then descends and traverses the Forbidden Glacier before ascending the knife-edge ridge with exposure on both sides. Climbers must move quickly, efficiently protect themselves, and be capable of 5.6 rock climbing with a medium pack over 12+ continuous hours.
overview: Links the summits of Mount Torment and Forbidden Peak along their connecting ridge, one of the premier moderate alpine traverses in the North Cascades. First climbed by Ed Cooper and Walt Sellers over a two-day push in July 1958, the traverse combines Torment's South Ridge/SE face, roughly a mile of exposed knife-edge ridge travel (the 'Sidewalk in the Sky'), and Forbidden Peak's West Ridge — the latter itself one of Roper & Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs of North America. The climbing is never harder than 5.6, but the traverse's length, glacier travel, and limited retreat options make it a serious full-value alpine day (or 2-day trip with a ridge bivy).

current.approach: From the Boston Basin trailhead pullout on Cascade River Road (~3,300 ft, opposite Johannesburg Mountain, roughly mile 22-23), follow the old abandoned mining road for about 0.75 mile to the historic mine site. From there an unmaintained but well-beaten climbers' path takes over, switchbacking steeply up through forest with four creek/stream crossings to treeline around 5,300 ft. Above the trees the path eases across heather benches and talus into Boston Basin proper; low camp sits around 5,300-5,500 ft and high camp around 6,400 ft (total roughly 2.5-3 miles and 3,000-3,300 ft gain from car to high camp, 2.5-4 hours). A North Cascades NP backcountry permit (Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount) is required to camp. From high camp, leave the trail and make a rising, rightward (northwest) traverse across talus, tundra, and slab steps, crossing a couple of small creeks/snowmelt channels, staying beneath the cliff bands below Torment and Sahale, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above. Rope up at the glacier's toe and cross it heading for the notch that marks the base of Torment's climbing (on the standard line this is the same notch that starts the South Ridge). Watch for crevasses and a moat at the glacier's edge that can require careful stepping or a short awkward move to reach rock; a picket, axe, and crampons for the first person are worth carrying. Biting flies are notorious in Boston Basin in mid-summer, early-season snow can obscure the creek crossings and add avalanche exposure on the traverse, and whiteout conditions make the basin-to-glacier traverse genuinely easy to get lost in.
approach_variant_names: Boston Basin high camp and the Taboo Glacier
current.descent: The traverse finishes by descending Forbidden Peak, not Torment, so 'descent' here means the way off Forbidden's summit back to Boston Basin. From Forbidden's summit, downclimb and make about 3 rappels down the West Ridge (mostly in-situ slings on horns/blocks, some natural gear placements) back down to the West Ridge Notch below the false summit. From the notch, continue down the standard Forbidden couloir system known as the Cat Scratch Gullies - multiple parallel loose gullies separated by rock ribs; the accepted trick is to stay on the rib between gullies rather than descending gully bottoms, which funnel rockfall. Trip reports are inconsistent on exact rappel count here because it depends heavily on snow coverage and how much is downclimbed versus rappelled: parties report anywhere from about 5 to 10 rappels through this section (7 is the most commonly cited figure), generally on a mix of slung horns/chockstones and a few fixed anchors, with a 60m rope recommended (most individual raps are short enough for 30m but the last is longer). Do not skip anchors that look short - a couple of the short ones are there because the next station isn't visible. This funnels back down to the Forbidden-Torment glacier remnant and snowfields, from which you rejoin the Boston Basin traverse. All told, budget roughly 3 (West Ridge) + 5-7 (Cat Scratch) = about 8-10 rappels for the full descent. The waterfall-polished slabs just below the glacier at the bottom of this system have caught out descending parties (fatalities have occurred here) - downclimb them very carefully or locate the rappel anchors rather than improvising a scramble.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from 0.4 to 2 inches, a set of nuts, about 8 alpine draws with slings, and two ropes for the rappels.
current.pro_needs: Protection on the rock steps is reasonable, but much of the traverse is moderate, exposed, run-out terrain where efficient movement matters more than gear. The snow sections take occasional pickets.
bivy: Torment Basin camp below the southeast face

name: Mount Townsend Trail (standard)
beta: From the Upper Trailhead the trail switchbacks up through old-growth hemlock/fir with a rhododendron understory, crosses a couple of seasonal streams in the first 1.5 miles, then eases into ridge walking with early views. Around 2.5 miles it reaches Camp Windy/Windy Lake amid wildflower meadows, then climbs a final steady, switchbacked pitch above treeline to the open, windswept summit plateau. The Lower Trailhead adds about 2 extra round-trip miles and roughly 500 extra feet of gain via the same trail corridor. There is no scrambling or hands-on terrain on the standard route; the only technical consideration is wind/weather exposure once above Camp Windy.
overview: Mount Townsend is one of the most-visited summits in the northeastern Olympics, rising above the Quilcene valley in the Buckhorn Wilderness of Olympic National Forest. The maintained Mt. Townsend Trail (#839) climbs through old-growth Douglas-fir/rhododendron forest, crosses a series of increasingly open, avalanche-scoured ravines, and breaks into subalpine meadows near Camp Windy (2.6 mi) before meeting the Silver Lake Trail junction (3 mi) and reaching the open, wind-scoured south summit (4 mi, roughly 6,260-6,280 ft). The south summit is the true high point; the lower north summit (about 6,212 ft) lies a short walk farther along the crest. On clear days the summit gives a full panorama of the Olympic high country (Mount Constance, Mount Deception, The Brothers), the Cascades, Hood Canal, Puget Sound, and the San Juan Islands. The combination of a short approach, no technical difficulty, and outsized views makes it one of the most popular day hikes/easy scrambles on the Olympic Peninsula.

current.approach: Start at the Mt. Townsend Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,300 ft), reached via Forest Road 27 off Penny Creek Road out of Quilcene — the trailhead has a small gravel lot and a Buckhorn Wilderness boundary sign where Trail #839 begins. From the lot, the trail climbs immediately into dense, heavily wooded old-growth forest via the first of three switchback sets; this opening stretch is the steepest sustained grade on the route and stays shaded most of the way. After the initial switchbacks the trail eases through forest before a second switchback section, then a third set of steep, fully sun-exposed switchbacks that break out onto the crest of a ridge — this exposed stretch is the hottest, most water-demanding part of the hike in summer, so carry all the water you need (there is no reliable creek crossing directly on-trail; the small streams crossed in the first mile or so are often dry by late summer, so shallow Windy Lake by Camp Windy is the last water). At about 5,300 ft, roughly 2.6 miles in, an unmarked spur trail branches off to Windy Lake/Camp Windy, a common rest stop and the last reliable flat ground before the alpine section. Continuing on the main trail, at about 5,500 ft you reach the junction with the Silver Lakes Trail #842 — stay right (straight/uphill) to continue to the summit; the left fork toward Silver Lakes involves loose, unmaintained scrambling and is not the standard route. From this junction the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the trail's grade eases considerably for the final ~1 mile to the broad, flat summit ridge (6,282 ft), passing through increasingly open wildflower meadows with the last quarter-mile crossing mostly open, low-angle grassy/rocky tundra. No technical terrain or exposure is encountered on the standard route; the main hazards are heat/sun exposure on the third switchback set, lingering snow patches on the upper meadows into early summer (which can obscure the tread and create a slip hazard on a steep sidehill), and occasional route-finding uncertainty at the Silver Lakes junction if signage is missing.
approach_variant_names: Mount Townsend Trail #839 from the Upper Trailhead
Little Quilcene Trail over Little River Summit
current.descent: Descend via the same Trail #839 back to the Upper Trailhead — this is a straightforward out-and-back with no technical downclimbing, exposure, or rappelling anywhere on the route. From the summit meadows, retrace the trail down through the Silver Lakes Trail junction (stay right/downhill on #839), past the Windy Lake spur, and back down through the three switchback sections to the trailhead. The only descent-specific cautions are the same as on the way up: the exposed third (lowest) switchback set can be loose underfoot with pea gravel over hardpack, making for slippery footing especially with a full pack or in wet conditions, and lingering snow on the upper meadow section in early season can make the tread hard to follow on the descent if you're moving in fog or flat light — carrying a GPS track or map is prudent before mid-July in high-snow years. No rope or rappel gear is needed for this route at any point.
current.pro_needs: None; this is a hiking/scrambling trail with no technical climbing.
current.rope_note: No rope required. Maintained Forest Trail #839, Class 1-2 throughout; summit is exposed/windy but non-technical.

name: Northeast Ridge
beta: The Northeast Ridge is the one genuinely 'moderate' way up an otherwise defended peak. From a col/bivy site above Thornton Lakes, the route crosses a shrinking glacier remnant and a loose gully to gain the ridge crest, then follows roughly 9-12 belayed pitches (mostly easy 5th class, with a runout 5.6 traverse and the signature 5.7 offwidth crux) plus short simul-climbed/scrambled sections along an exposed, towered ridge to the summit. The descent reverses the ridge with a long series of rappels and downclimbing back to the col.
overview: A long, sustained alpine rock route climbing Mount Triumph's northeast-facing ridge from a high bivy col above Thornton Lakes to the small, airy summit — mostly 4th and low-5th class ridge climbing over towers and a knife-edge crest, capped by a well-known 5.7 offwidth crux near the top.

current.approach: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east to the Thornton Lakes Road spur (near milepost 117, just west of Newhalem) and follow the rough, unpaved, high-clearance road about 5 miles to the Thornton Lakes Trailhead (~2,500 ft). Hike the Thornton Lakes Trail — an old logging-road grade for the first ~2 miles, then steeper trail up to the ridge/pass (~4,900 ft) above the lakes — then descend to the lake outlet (~4,400-4,486 ft). Traverse the brushy, sometimes-faint climbers' path around the east/south side of middle Thornton Lake, then climb a long, loose scree/talus gully (roughly 1,200 ft of gain) to a col around 5,750-5,840 ft that serves as the standard bivy site.
approach_variant_names: Thornton Lakes Trail, the middle lake and the gully to the bivy col
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb roughly 30 ft off the north side of the notch to easier rock, then reverse the ridge via a long string of rappels (double-rope where two ropes are carried) interspersed with downclimbing — accounts report anywhere from about 7 to 10 rappels total, including a double-rope rappel off the crux crack pitch — back down to the bivy col. Existing slings and rap rings are present at most stations but the rock is loose, so back up or replace suspect anchors. From the col, reverse the approach gully and climbers' path back around Thornton Lake and out the Thornton Lakes Trail to the trailhead. On a late-September descent the third rappel used nearly all of a 60 m rope (a 57 m rope fell short), and some of the older anchors needed to be cut away and replaced; carry spare cord and full-length ropes.
current.detailed_rack: A single 60-70m rope suffices for the moderate pitches, though many parties carry two ropes (twins or a rope + tag line) to allow full-length double-rope rappels on the descent. Rack light: nuts, a set of TCUs/small cams, and cams up to a #2-3 Camalot (a #3 is useful for the crux offwidth), 12+ alpine draws for the many horns and flakes, and several cordelettes/long slings for building anchors and backing up old tat at rap stations.
current.pro_needs: Protection is generally adequate on the low-5th ridge (horizontal slots, flakes, and horns for slings) but sparse and runout on a couple of the harder pitches, notably a 5.6 traverse; the crux 5.7 offwidth/crack takes cams to #2-3.

name: West Route
beta: In 1938, Sigurd Hall's first-ascent party found a bench on the west side with a roughly 35-degree longitudinal dip that led up onto Triumph's south face; a ledge then crosses the face to the southeast shoulder, from which easier ground leads to the summit. A more recent trip report describing a similar 'West Face-Southeast Face' line notes angling up rock/heather benches alongside the 'Great White Slabs' to a broad talus shoulder, then Class 4 rock and heather to a large southeast-slanting ramp, and a final Class 5 gully/slot (poor rock, minimal protection) to the summit crest.
overview: The technically easiest way up Mount Triumph but the least climbed line: a long Class 4 route up the mountain's west side and south face to the southeast shoulder, reached via the much longer and rougher Triumph Pass climbers' route rather than the popular Thornton Lakes approach used for the Northeast Ridge.

current.approach: Reached via the longer, rougher Triumph Pass climbers' route rather than the standard Thornton Lakes approach used for the Northeast Ridge; used far less often and much less documented than the NE Ridge approach.
current.descent: Reverse the route with a long series of rappels (double- and single-rope) back down the southeast ramp and west-side benches.
current.pro_needs: Minimal and poor protection reported on the final Class 5 summit gully/slot; better pro lower on the route in horizontal slots.

name: South/East Scramble
beta: From a base camp or day-hike start at Watson Lakes, leave the maintained trail and work up open slopes on the mountain's north side toward the notch between the lower East Peak and the true (western) summit. Cross a short but steep snow finger / remnant glacier apron in the notch (ice axe and crampons or microspikes advisable for most of the season), then scramble loose, mossy class 3 terrain west along the south side of the ridge and along a narrow, knife-edge ridge crest to the true summit. Most parties descend the same way; some instead drop east onto the shrinking Watson Glacier to shortcut back toward the lakes.
overview: Mount Watson (6,221 ft) is the highest point in the 14,666-acre Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, rising above the sub-alpine Anderson and Watson Lakes basins on the Mt. Baker Ranger District west of Baker Lake. Its nearest higher neighbor is Bacon Peak, 2.6 mi to the east, and a small glacial remnant (Watson Glacier) clings to its north slopes. The peak is reached via the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail (#611); above the lakes the route leaves the trail for open heather benches and talus, climbing to a saddle around 5,900 ft on the summit ridge before a short, steep, tree-and-rock scramble to a narrow, airy summit block with real exposure on both sides (Class 2-3, with the final ridge occasionally handlined). It's a popular combo objective with an overnight at the lakes.

current.approach: Park at the Watson Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS Road 1107 (elev. ~4,300 ft), reached via Baker Lake Road (FS-11) south around Baker Lake on FS-1106 and out FS-1107 to road's end. From the trailhead, follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 into the woods; at about 1 mile you'll pass the junction with the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1 (stay straight/right for Watson Lakes). Around 1.5-2 miles, at roughly 4,700 ft, a second junction splits: right drops 0.5 mile to lower Anderson Lake, while the left fork climbs 0.5 mile to a small saddle entering the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping to the Watson Lakes (4,400 ft) near 2.5-3 miles in. The lakes are notoriously buggy in summer and are the last reliable water — treat before filling up, since there's no dependable source higher on the mountain. From Watson Lakes the maintained trail ends and the route becomes an open, cairned/boot-path climbers' route: leave the basin and climb talus (and snow well into summer) on Watson's north/west slopes toward the ridge crest. The standard and easiest line follows the widest gully east of the peak up to a saddle at about 5,900 ft on the ridge; a western gully alternative has a dangerous moat and rotten snow bridge late-season and should be avoided. From the 5,900-ft saddle, traverse along the ridge and across a steep slope to wrap around the base of the summit block. A short, loose class 2-3 dirt-and-rock gully (10-15 ft) gains the true summit ridge, which is a narrow (~30 ft), exposed class 2-3 catwalk with real drop-off on both sides — a hand line is commonly carried and recommended for this final airy section. Total round trip runs roughly 7-9.5 miles with 2,500-3,000 ft gain depending on exact trailhead/camp and route-finding; parties camping partway (e.g., ~5,400 ft on the north slopes) shorten the summit day considerably. Route-finding above the lakes is the main approach hazard in poor visibility since the line is unmarked talus/snow rather than trail.
approach_variant_names: Watson Lakes Trailhead, Trail #611 and the east gully to the saddle
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent line in its entirety — this is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling (rappels: 0). From the summit, downclimb the exposed, narrow class 2-3 summit ridge (many parties use a hand line here) back down the short loose gully to the base of the summit block, then traverse back around the block and along the ridge to the 5,900-ft saddle. From the saddle, descend the east gully (the same talus/snow line used on the way up — avoid the west gully's moat/snow-bridge hazard) back into the basin above Watson Lakes, then pick up the maintained Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 at the lakes for the hike out to the trailhead, passing back through the two junctions (the ~4,700-ft Anderson/Watson Lakes fork, then the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1 junction at 1 mile from the trailhead). Descent times are typically close to ascent times (roughly 3+ hours from summit to car), consistent with a straightforward if loose reversal. Descent-specific hazards: loose talus and scree in the gully below the saddle, glissade/postholing risk on residual snow into midsummer, rotten moats/snow bridges if the west-side line is mistakenly used, and route-finding across the open, unmarked basin and ridge in flat light or fog — the exposed summit-ridge downclimb remains the technical crux in both directions.
current.detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb for most parties. Some parties carry a short rope/basic glacier gear for the small Watson Glacier remnant depending on conditions.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection or rappel stations are documented; this is unroped class 3 scrambling with one short, steep snow/glacier crossing. A rope is optional insurance for the glacier apron in early season, not standard gear for most summer ascents.
bivy: Camp on slopes below Mount Watson (~5,400 ft)
Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
current.rope_note: Overall non-technical scramble; the final summit block is a ~30ft, Class 2-3 ridge with severe exposure on both sides, and a fixed line is commonly recommended for this section specifically.

name: Standard Route
beta: From the Tubal Cain Trailhead, a well-graded trail leads about 6 miles to Buckhorn Lake, the last water source and jumping-off point for the summit. Above the lake the route leaves the trail, climbing through avalanche-damaged timber to treeline near 5,800 ft, then ascending loose scree and talus -- either angling toward the roughly 6,420-ft saddle between Iron Mountain and Worthington, or straight up a wide gully south of the lake -- to the peak's open summit plateau. A final short scramble up a rock fin, with some exposure, gains the true summit. Overall the route is Class 2 with a Class 3 summit block, but loose rock and off-trail routefinding make it feel harder than the grade suggests to many parties.
overview: Mount Worthington (6,938 ft) is a double-summited peak (main summit plus Northeast Worthington, 6,880 ft) in the Buckhorn Wilderness of the eastern Olympic Mountains, Jefferson County — reached via the Tubal Cain Trail system, not via Royal Basin/Gray Wolf Ridge (a separate trailhead and drainage to the west). It sits on the ridge between Iron Mountain (0.76 mi SW) and Hawk Peak (NE), 1.3 mi northeast of higher Buckhorn Mountain. Originally called Copper Peak after the Tubal Cain copper mine worked at its northern base in the early 1900s, it was renamed for local pioneer William J. Worthington. It's a popular non-technical scramble objective, commonly linked with Iron Mountain and NE Worthington in a single ridge trip staged from Buckhorn Lake.

current.approach: Start at the Tubal Cain Trailhead (elev. ~3,300 ft, reached via FR 2870/2880), and follow the Tubal Cain Trail #840 (Copper Creek drainage) south. The trail climbs gently through second-growth and old-growth conifer forest, gaining roughly 1,900 ft over the first ~5.5-6 miles. At about 3 miles, pass the signed junction with the Tull Canyon Trail #847 (a steep 0.6-mile side spur to a 1952 B-17 crash site) and continue straight on #840. Around 0.5 mile past that junction the trail crosses Copper Creek near the historic Tubal Cain Mine tailings (last reliable, easy water before the lake), then switchbacks up through subalpine meadows toward Buckhorn Pass. Watch for the unsigned or lightly-signed spur (near ~5,200 ft, roughly 5.5-6 miles in) that drops left to Buckhorn Lake -- it's easy to miss, so watch for the left turn to Buckhorn Lake. Follow this spur down to the lake, which is the last dependable water source before the summit push. From the south end of Buckhorn Lake the maintained tread disappears; cross the inlet stream/waterfall at the head of the lake and pick up a faint boot path heading southwest into avalanche-damaged timber (expect blowdown and light bushwhacking). This opens into a broad, flat bench of avalanche debris about 200 ft above the lake -- the true start of the off-trail scramble. From there climb a wide talus/scree gully trending south then curving east, breaking treeline around 5,800 ft (roughly 700 ft above the lake), where the going turns to loose rock and light class 2-3 scrambling. Angle east/southeast up increasingly loose slopes to gain the Iron-Worthington col at approximately 6,420 ft. Hazards on this leg: avalanche debris and blowdown near the lake, sustained loose scree/talus underfoot above treeline (helmet recommended for rockfall from parties above), and route-finding through the faint, unmarked path -- a GPS track or detailed written beta is strongly advised since cairns are sparse. From the Iron-Worthington col, angle northeast up open slopes to the base of Worthington's summit fin; the final class 3 scramble drops a few feet left of the ridge crest to a short (~10 ft) crack, then follows the top of the fin to the true summit.
approach_variant_names: Tubal Cain Trail #840 and Buckhorn Lake
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line rather than continuing the Iron-Worthington ridge traverse. From the summit plateau, downclimb the short technical step below the true summit -- a class 3 face with good holds, done as an 'up-and-down climb' on the same line used to ascend (an alternate, slightly easier low-exposure line exists around the NE corner of the summit block for parties that want to avoid re-downclimbing the ascent face). There are no fixed rappel anchors, bolts, or established rappel stations on this route -- this is a walk-off/downclimb peak, not a rappel route. From the base of the summit block, descend southwest back to the Iron-Worthington col, then drop into the wide scree/talus gully on the west side of the col -- this is the standout feature of the descent, offering a fast, low-angle boot-ski through loose scree and talus back down to treeline and the avalanche-debris bench above Buckhorn Lake. Below treeline, re-cross the inlet stream, pick up the boot path back to the Buckhorn Lake spur, and rejoin the maintained Tubal Cain Trail #840 for the ~5.5-6 mile, ~1,900 ft-loss walk out to the trailhead. Because the summit block is a short, low-exposure downclimb rather than a rappel, and no rope is needed for the descent (a rope is optional/prudent for less confident scramblers on the way up, not for a rappel), rappels = 0.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear for the standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: None for the standard line
bivy: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington

name: Standard Route / South Side
beta: From the base of the tower, a single pitch of mid-5th-class (roughly 5.5) climbing leads directly to Mushroom Tower's small, exposed, lopsided summit block. It is commonly combined with nearby Big Kangaroo and/or Melted Tower, which share the same Kangaroo Ridge approach, for a bigger day out.
overview: Mushroom Tower is a slender granite tower at the north end of Kangaroo Ridge, immediately north of Big Kangaroo (8,280 ft), above Washington Pass on the North Cascades Highway (SR 20). It takes its name from a blocky, overhanging summit block that must be gained via a short, exposed step-across — a memorable finish to an otherwise moderate low-5th-class scramble/climb.

current.approach: From the large pullout on the inside of the Hairpin Turn on SR-20 (~Milepost 163, roughly 5,150 ft, just below Washington Pass), drop off the highway shoulder and ford Early Winters Creek directly across from the parking area — expect wet feet in early-season high water; by mid-to-late summer it braids down to an easy rock-hop. From the far bank, head straight up into timber on climber's-left of the obvious drainage gully that falls from Kangaroo Ridge; a boot-path stays in the trees rather than fighting brush in the gully bottom itself. As the trees thin, keep to the left side of the gully and follow it onto the ridge crest above, mixing dirt/heather benches with short bouts of easy Class 2-3 scrambling. This is the shared approach line for all of the Kangaroo Ridge towers (Big Kangaroo, Half Moon, Mushroom Tower) and packs about 3,000 ft of gain into well under 2 miles, so it is steep and sustained the whole way — plan on 2.5-4 hours up for a party unfamiliar with it. Where the ridge steepens below the final rock tiers, traverse left beneath the base of the wall and climb a band of steep snow (a snowfinger that lingers on this shaded aspect well into summer) to reach the notch/base directly under Mushroom Tower's summit block; an ice axe is standard here and crampons are worth carrying in early season, when this stretch can hold enough snow to kick steps the whole way. There is no reliable water above the initial creek ford, so treat that crossing as your last easy fill-up. There is no maintained trail or trail number above the highway — it is entirely a climber's boot-path, and route-finding is straightforward in clear weather (aim for the mushroom-capped tower on the skyline) but unforgiving in fog or whiteout given the mix of gully, timber, and traverse terrain.
current.descent: The route tops out with a short, exposed step/traverse across a gap just below the true summit block, which is the technical crux and can be wet or verglassed when snow is still sitting on top of the tower. Descent from the summit is a single rappel — well under one rope length — off a fixed anchor of two old 1/4-inch bolts placed by Fred Beckey's party during the June 1942 first ascent of the Kangaroo Ridge towers. Treat it as decades-old hardware: inspect it closely before trusting it and back it up (or extend/replace) if you're carrying the means to do so. A standard doubled rope (e.g., a 60m rope folded to give 30m per strand, or even a doubled 30m rope) reaches with room to spare; a single-strand rappel on a 30m+ rope would also work if that suits your retrieval plan. The rappel lands on south-side scramble terrain; from there, downclimb/scramble back to the notch and reverse the ascent traverse and snowfinger to the head of the approach gully. Descend the same climber's-left line used on the way up — the gully commonly holds snow late into the season and can be partially glissaded, which speeds the descent but carries runout and rockfall-channel exposure once the snow softens in the afternoon sun, so timing matters. Continue down through timber to Early Winters Creek, re-ford, and you're back at the Hairpin Turn pullout. This is not a walk-off: even though the technical climbing is short (2 pitches), the exposed summit step and the fixed-anchor rappel mean a rope, harness, and rappel device are mandatory gear, not optional. Round-trip car-to-car time for a party familiar with the route runs roughly 6-8 hours.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack suffices for the short technical climbing: a small set of cams, a few nuts, and 4-6 slings. Carry a couple of spare slings or rap rings to supplement or back up the summit's two old 1/4-inch bolt anchors, whose exact condition isn't documented.
current.pro_needs: Light trad rack plus extra tat for the aged fixed rappel anchor; crampons/axe for early-season snow on the approach gully.

name: Mutchler Peak Scramble
beta: Mutchler Peak sits at the east end of the long southeast ridge that runs off Snowking Mountain, above the Kindy Creek/Mutchler Creek drainage. Parties reach it either by continuing the Kindy Ridge approach used for Snowking's East Ridge (3rd class, Grade II) past the summit and along the connecting ridge/snowfields toward the Buckindy group, or from the south on the longer Green Mountain–Mount Misch–Mount Buckindy traverse, camping at the pass between Kindy and Buck Creeks before crossing to Mutchler. Terrain is a mix of steep heather, talus, snow/glacier remnants, and low-class rock; one documented traverse rappelled over a cornice to reach the peak.
overview: Mutchler Peak (7,150 ft; referenced in some older trip reports as 'Snowqueen') is a remote summit in the Buckindy Group of the Cascade River backcountry, part of the rugged, semi-glaciated ridge system southeast of Marblemount that also includes Snowking Mountain (7,433'), Mount Buckindy (7,320'), Mount Misch (7,435'), Bruseth Mountain (7,220'), and Mount Chaval to the east. There is no maintained trail to Mutchler; it sits in roadless country between the Cascade River and Suiattle River drainages and is almost always climbed cross-country as part of a longer Buckindy Range traverse rather than as a standalone day trip.

current.approach: Park at the Cascade River Road washout roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount, about 100 yards past the Cascade River crossing near the FR 1570 junction (signed for Kindy Ridge/Found Lake). The old FR 1570 spur is now permanently closed to vehicles, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek at roughly 1,150-1,400 ft — parties note the washed-out culvert and downed timber (one log up to 4 ft across) blocking the road about 0.8 mile in. Follow the old road/boot path, crossing several windfalls, to an old firepit near a reliable creek (last easy water before the ridge). From the firepit the unmaintained climbers' path turns steep immediately, threading old-growth forest on exposed roots with occasional spur tracks around blowdown; expect the tread to fade into debris in places — this stretch to the Found Peak area (roughly 2.5 miles, gaining ~2,500-3,000 ft) is the main route-finding crux of the approach. The path dips to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft where the boot path is easy to lose; parties often end up scrambling 300-400 ft above the pass before relocating the trail, then follow it up through grass and boulders (~600 ft) into a meadow with Found Lake below (pools here are not reliably potable). From there the route climbs over Point 5695 and drops to a second saddle before joining Kindy Ridge proper: a broad, mostly open granite ridge combining faint tread and easy slab-hopping, steep but non-technical, with constant views toward Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak, and the Cyclone Lake basin. Camps are commonly made near 6,200 ft on the ridge or down at Cyclone Lake (a strikingly turquoise tarn-fed lake); a small stream south of the ridge camp and a tarn just above Cyclone Lake are the best water sources up high. From the ridge/Cyclone Lake basin, Mutchler Peak's summit block is reached by heather and blocky rock slopes rising out of the basin — moderate Class 2-3 scrambling with some loose rock near the top; no published figure gives the car-to-summit distance for Mutchler itself, but Snowking, reached by the same approach over Kindy Ridge, is roughly 16-18 miles round trip. Because the approach is entirely unmaintained (no official trail, no numbered Forest Service trail), competent off-trail navigation is required, and this is a long, full-day-plus approach — most parties treat it as an overnight rather than a single push.
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down Mutchler's heather and blocky rock flanks into the Cyclone Lake basin, then back up and over the Found Peak/Kindy Ridge saddle system to the 4,800 ft saddle and down through the old-growth/windfall section to the firepit and abandoned FR 1570 roadbed, then out to the Cascade River Road washout. This is a walk-off/downclimb the entire way — no rappelling is involved on the scramble route or its descent. The main descent hazards are route-finding (the boot path through the meadow/saddle area above Found Peak is easy to lose in both directions and there are cliff bands nearby to avoid), loose rock and heather on the steep upper slopes off Mutchler's summit, and fatigue-driven navigation errors on the long unmaintained stretch back to the road, especially if daylight runs short — at least one trip report specifically mentions avoiding a creek-bed shortcut on the way out after dark in favor of staying on the known road/trail line.
current.detailed_rack: No rock rack is needed. The standard line is a Class 2-3 scramble up heather and blocky rock, and parties reach the summit unroped; no rack is carried.
current.pro_needs: No protection is needed on the standard line: it is a Class 2-3 scramble with no roped glacier travel, and there are no fixed anchors or bolts on the scrambling sections.
bivy: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found online. Class 3 scrambles of this type typically require no rope.

name: Nature's Way
beta: Pitch 1 climbs easy granite ramps and blocks up a V-gully to a large ledge; pitch 2 works through a series of ledges to a crux rightward-slanting seam at the fourth bolt; pitch 3 is the route's namesake objective - a sustained hand crack with lieback/stem moves to a knob and roughly 12 feet of continuous undercling to chains atop a flake.
overview: A short, 3-pitch line finishing up an obvious hand crack soaring above the South Face's granite apron - the most recently established named route on the wall.

current.approach: From the grassy saddle bivy, cross the granite apron past the start of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer to two-bolt ring anchors on the opposite wall.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
current.descent: 3 rappels down the route via two-bolt chain anchors at each belay.
current.detailed_rack: Double rack from .3"-.75" plus one 2" piece; two-bolt chain anchors at every belay.
current.pro_needs: Gear-protected crack climbing on pitch 3 backed by bolts on the crux seam of pitch 2.

name: NE Chimney
beta: The climbing is hard, sustained 5.9. Whether chockstones in the chimney offer protection every 20-30 ft through the crux has been debated since at least 2004 without a clear answer, so treat it as a serious, sparsely-protected lead. Pitch count and length are not recorded.
overview: A harder, sustained line up a chimney system on Molar Tooth's NE Face, rated 5.9.

current.approach: From the Cutthroat Trailhead (~4,500 ft, via SR-20 and FS Road 400 about 28 miles west of Winthrop), follow the Cutthroat Creek Trail/PCT toward Cutthroat Pass, then branch onto scree slopes to reach the base of the NE Face.

name: NE Couloir
beta: A sustained snow climb with a crux at the upper narrow section. Approximately 5-hour round trip from trailhead depending on conditions. Route requires good snow conditions and avalanche awareness.
overview: The longest and most continuous narrow snow gully on the left side of Tiffany's north face, averaging 40 degrees with steeper sections to 55 degrees.

current.approach: From Tiffany Springs Campground (6,760 ft), hike trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass (7,150 ft, ~45 min). From the pass, traverse SW/south along the east slope below the ridge crest to the small cirque at the base of the North Face (7,360 ft), then continue to the base of the couloir. Driving access: via Conconully/North Fork Salmon Creek (~21 mi, ~1 hr, rough road, 4WD recommended), via the South Fork/Baldy Pass (~30.6 mi, ~2 hr, 2WD gravel), or via the Methow Valley (~26.5 mi, ~1 hr, 2WD gravel).
approach_variant_names: Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass
current.descent: From the top of the couloir on the summit ridge, walk off via Tiffany's northwest ridge, then drop to the old unmaintained trail above Little Tiffany Lake, following it down to rejoin trail #373 near Honeymoon Pass and retracing the approach back to Tiffany Springs Campground. Allow roughly 5 hours round-trip from the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: If the snow is continuous, a rope with medium nuts and/or pickets is recommended for protection, particularly through the steeper mid- and upper-couloir sections.
current.pro_needs: An ice axe is essential. If the snow is continuous, bring a rope and medium nuts and pickets for protection of the crux section.

name: Northwest Ridge (from Needle Peak)
beta: On August 19, 2006, Blake Herrington and Tim Haider left the Agnes Creek Trail at Swamp Creek and climbed Needle Peak via its North Ridge, then continued along the connecting ridgeline, making the first ascents of the North and South Anonymity Towers, before climbing the Dark Glacier to a bivouac atop Dark Peak. The next day they continued the ridge crest to Bonanza Peak's west and main summits. The overall linkup was rated Grade V, 5.8, with rock along the crest that is wild and highly variable in quality; no separate grade, pitch count, or length is available for the Needle Peak segment alone.
overview: Bonanza Peak's Northwest Ridge (V 5.8) is a long, rarely repeated link-up that reaches Washington's highest non-volcanic summit from the northwest. This version starts from Swamp Creek off the Agnes Creek trail: it climbs Needle Peak by its north ridge, carries over the North and South Anonymity Towers at low fifth class, crosses the Dark Glacier to Dark Peak, and then follows the high, knife-edged crest joining Dark Peak to Bonanza's west and main summits, with the hardest climbing (5.8) on the last two pitches. It descends the Mary Green Glacier toward Holden.

current.approach: From Stehekin (reached only by passenger boat or floatplane up Lake Chelan — no road access), follow the Agnes Creek Trail upstream and leave the maintained trail at Swamp Creek to travel cross-country onto Needle Peak's north side and gain the North Ridge.
current.descent: This is a long ridge traverse that links Needle Peak, Dark Peak and the crest to Bonanza, so there is no easy retreat once committed; the way down is from the Bonanza summit ridge by the Mary Green Glacier route. Expect to descend that glacier in the evening after a full day on the crest, with heavy crevassing that calls for roped glacier travel and care in the dark. Continue down to the Holden Pass high camp and then out the Holden Lake trail to Holden Village. Do not start this traverse in unsettled weather, since backtracking along the crest is the only alternative.
current.detailed_rack: A 30m rope and a few slings cover a crux move or short rappel.
bivy: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain

name: New York Gully
beta: A popular Seattle-area winter mixed testpiece: a short approach off I-90 leads to a moderate lower gully, then progressively steeper mixed ground (up to M5-) through slabby, sometimes loose rock, finishing at a splitter 5.8 corner crack that was historically aided (A1-2) and has since been free-climbed. Conditions vary widely year to year — some seasons build fat ice through the gully, dry years leave it mostly rock/mixed with minimal screw placements. It sits on the edge of the Phantom Slide avalanche path, so timing relative to snowpack stability is as important as the climbing itself.
overview: New York Gully splits the NW Face of Snoqualmie Mountain, the most-climbed of five parallel ice/mixed lines on that wall (alongside Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, and LA Express). First climbed by Ruch and Cordery-Cotter in 1985 as a IV 5.8 A2 WI4 aid line, it's a roughly 700-ft alpine route following a prominent gully system to a distinctive 'box gully' feature, finishing with a steep corner pitch that was originally aided and first freed in 2004 at M5+/6-.

current.approach: Park in the Alpental groomer lot, about 200 ft past the main day-lot at the end of WA-906/Alpental Rd (reached via I-90 Exit 52). From the lot, walk up the open, south-facing hillside toward the Alpental waterfalls. At the base of the falls, cut left into the trees for roughly 100 ft and climb up through two steep, often snowed-up rock/cliff bands — this section is frequently booted or skinned by prior parties, and picking up an existing track through the thick timber makes a real difference in speed and route-finding; without one, expect slow going. After about 300 ft of gain, angle right onto the Phantom Slide itself, a broad avalanche path that is the defining feature (and hazard) of this approach: it slides regularly, including on skiers and climbers on the upper apron, so check the NWAC forecast beforehand and time your crossing/ascent to stable conditions rather than lingering on it. Climb the slide path to about 4,900 ft, then trend left and up through lower-angle, more open terrain to a notch on the NW shoulder/West Ridge near 5,200 ft. From the notch, downclimb roughly 200 vertical feet into the Thunder Creek cirque basin and traverse beneath the NW Face to the base of the gully system — note this face hosts five closely spaced ice/mixed lines (Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully, and LA Express), so confirm you're racking up below the correct one. No reliable water source along this approach in winter/spring conditions; plan to melt snow. Figure roughly 1.5–3 hours car-to-base depending on snowpack, track conditions, and party experience with the terrain.
approach_variant_names: Alpental groomer lot, the Phantom Slide, and the NW shoulder notch into Thunder Creek cirque
current.descent: From the top of the technical climbing (the crux mixed pitches, including the route's namesake 'box gully' section), downclimb easy snow angling to climber's right, then traverse up to a col between two gendarmes on the upper ridge. From that col, make one rappel from an established tree anchor — a single 60m rope reaches the bottom comfortably (many parties carry a 70m since it's also useful for simul-climbing/leading the route's 4 long pitches), dropping into the Enigma Gully, also known locally as the Slot couloir. This tree-anchor rappel is also the standard bail point if weather, conditions, or time force a retreat before topping out. From the base of the rappel, climb back up moderate snow in the Enigma/Slot gully to regain the main summit ridge near 6,200 ft, then walk the short remaining distance to Snoqualmie Mountain's true summit. From the summit, descend the standard Southwest Slopes scramble route: steep, loose scree and exposed rock past Cave Ridge, dropping toward the Source Lake basin and rejoining the Snow Lake/Source Lake trail back to the Alpental parking lot (this standard descent line is roughly 3,100 ft of its own elevation loss over about 1.9 miles one-way, and is considered a genuinely hard, sustained scramble in its own right, not just a walk-down). In good, stable snow conditions some parties instead ski or boot straight back down the Phantom Slide to the resort rather than taking the scree-and-scramble Southwest Slopes line. Total rappels on route: 1. Round trip is commonly 8–11 hours car-to-car.
current.detailed_rack: A single 60m rope plus a thin tag line (or a single 70m rope for simul-climbing sections) is standard. Rack to 2-3 inches including offset nuts and cams in the 0.2-0.5 in range for the P4/P5 dihedral and crack systems, a few knifeblade pitons for thin seams, and 3-4 ice screws (10-13cm) — screw count and size needs vary hugely with conditions, from essentially unnecessary in dry years to fully useful in a fat-ice season. No bolts on route; some fixed pitons exist at select stances. Bring extra slings for tree/horn anchors on the lower gully and for the walk-off.
current.pro_needs: Protection is a mix of thin-crack gear (offsets, small cams, knifeblades) for the rock sections and screws for whatever ice is present that season; the crux corner crack takes good small-to-medium cams and was historically bridged with two moves of fixed-gear aid (A1-2) before being freed.

name: Northwest Corner (Boving-Pollack Route)
beta: The Northwest Corner is a well-established four-to-five pitch route that ascends the natural corner system on the northwest aspect of North Early Winters Spire. This is one of the most popular routes on the peak, known for reliable rock quality and manageable protection requirements. The route follows a clear line with sustained climbing throughout.
overview: Northwest Corner (Boving-Pollack), 5.9+ III, is the classic moderate outing on North Early Winters Spire, the northern/lower of the two Early Winters Spires in the Liberty Bell Group at Washington Pass. First climbed by Paul Boving and Steve Pollack on September 25, 1976, it follows a corner system, the well-known 'Zig-Zag Flakes' pitch, and a burly offwidth up the peak's northwest aspect in 4-5 pitches (roughly 500 ft of climbing), finishing with a 4th-class traverse around a roof to the summit. It's one of the most popular moderate alpine rock routes at Washington Pass alongside the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell and the South Arete on South Early Winters Spire.

current.approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of Hwy 20 (elev. ~5,400 ft), about one mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook and roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop. Follow the well-graded Blue Lake Trail southwest through subalpine forest. At about 1.4-1.5 miles, watch for a signed junction: the main trail continues straight toward Blue Lake, while a climber's path splits left/south, signed for "Liberty Bell Trail #727 – Climbing Access," reached just past a small stream/meadow that is the last reliable water source before the basin. Take the climber's trail, which switchbacks up through slabs, talus, and heather meadows into the Liberty Bell/Early Winters basin beneath the west faces of the spire group — roughly another 0.5 mile and 1,000-1,300 ft of gain, putting total approach distance at about 2 miles with 1,300-1,600 ft of gain from the car (most parties report 1-2 hours). From the upper basin, continue scrambling/traversing north along the base of North Early Winters Spire's west side to a distinctive corner/crack system that leads to a tree-covered ledge — the shared start for the Northwest Corner and West Face. Hazards: lingering snow and occasional avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully well into June (many early-season parties boot or ski the lower approach), talus and slab sections with some route-finding among braided climbers' paths, and no dependable water once past the stream near the Liberty Bell Trail junction, so fill up there.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail, then north along the base of the west side
current.descent:
Two established ways off the summit; both are widely used and either works, but they return you to different spots relative to a gear stash at the base.

Bolted West Face rappel line (most direct back to packs at the base of NW Corner/West Face): from the summit, downclimb/walk skier's-left to the top of a clean, purpose-bolted rappel line down the right side of the West Face. Six bolted (2-bolt) rappel stations in a nearly direct line bring you back down to essentially the same spot where you left your pack at the base of the route. Pulls are reported as clean and the line is efficient — regulars find it a breeze. A single 60m rope is just barely sufficient (one station, reportedly the 3rd rappel, is tight enough that you may need to reach down to clip your PAS/daisy to the anchor and feed rope through your device to reach it); a 70m rope removes that squeeze and is the more comfortable choice. No natural anchors needed on this line — it's fully bolted.

Classic notch/chockstone descent (South/Southwest Gully): downclimb and rappel the south side into the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then continue down the Southwest Gully (the South Early Winter Spire "Chockstone Route" descent). This runs three single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the notch/gully (which often holds snow even in summer), followed by one spectacular, largely free-hanging double-rope rappel down and past a huge chockstone (~50 ft of air), then a final short rappel (~30 ft, off a tree anchor) or downclimb/scramble to reach the base. Total is about 4-5 rappels on this line. Anchors are natural/fixed slings around the chockstone and trees rather than bolts — inspect webbing before trusting it. Summit-to-base time on this descent is typically around 1.5-2 hours. This option is the standard descent if you climbed a route on the south/southwest side, or as a backup if the West Face bolt line is congested or iced.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles 0.75"-3" (BD sizes 2-4), a single 4" (#5) piece, and singles from fingers to 1" cover the lower corner pitches; the P4 offwidth wants the #4-5 pieces though the climbing is more secure than it looks via face-smears/arm-bars even where gear is sparse. Carry several extra-long slings for P2, P3, and the P5 roof traverse to control rope drag. A 60m rope is the minimum for the bolted West Face rappel descent.
current.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack to #4 Camalot with doubles in the 2-4" range, plus a single #5; a 60m (70m more comfortable) rope if descending via the bolted rappel line.
